items.descriptionOriginal: In a piazza in Rome on a lovely summer evening, an elderly duo set up a speaker and pressed “play.” The familiar beat and guitar intro of Michael Jackson ‘s “Beat It” filled the air, and the man and woman began to dance . They didn’t dance randomly, but in unison with simple choreographed dance moves. No camera set up. No tip jar. Just two older Italians enjoying their evening in the piazza and bringing joy to themselves and others. The Tour Guy , a tour operator headquartered in Rome with tours across Europe, shared the delightful dance clip on Instagram, where it had been viewed more than five million times. View this post on Instagram They just wanted to dance The video was filmed on August 6, 2026, at approximately 7:00 p.m., by Sean Finelli . The caption of the video explained the scene: ⁠ “A man and a woman gathered in Piazza Testaccio, played Michael Jackson, and did a choreographed dance. They did this for about 20 mins to 5 or so different songs. Each dance was slightly different, but choreographed. They didn’t have a hat out to collect tips, they didn’t have anyone filming, they didn’t even want the video I took which I offered to share with them after, they just wanted to dance. ⁠ At the end, they walked in separate directions and that was it. I’ve been to this piazza almost daily the last two weeks and a few times per month this summer. I’ve never seen anyone do anything like this here. If you’re not familiar, Piazza Testaccio is one of the last remaining places in Rome where you can still find children playing each night and locals hanging out. The sense of community here is still strong.” A special moment in a special place Testaccio is a historically working-class Rome neighborhood built around the city’s ancient river port, and its name comes from the Latin word for the amphora shards that form Monte Testaccio . Some people in the comments concurred that Testaccio is something special:ng special: “I randomly came across this piazza one day and sat down to enjoy the shade, the children, the community. I was travelling alone and it was this beautiful moment of experiencing something not ‘for tourists.’ I spoke to no one, took no photos, so perhaps I got to blend in, just for a moment. ” Skyline of Rome, Italy. Photo credit: Canva “Best neighborhood, stayed there for a month was able to participate in the feste and pilgrimage around the neighborhood in May…l cant wait to return, love love loved it.” “I live nearby, when the good season starts they go to the park near Testaccio and dance for one hour or more, they practice a lot ! We love them.” Here for the vitality, not the virality People loved the carefree way the pair danced without any expectation of audience, virality, or recognition. “Congratulations to these two excellent dancers! So much beauty in this simple video.” “I love this! They’re doing it for their own happiness!” “How cute are they! This is what aging well looks like. Better than many young people. Congratulations to them. ” “Love this! They’re clearly living their best life doing what they enjoy ” “Looks like step aerobics. I love it. Still staying active and keeping it fresh. Italians are the best.” Meet Pasquale, the dancer People have wondered who the pair are. The man in the video showed up in the comments to thank everyone: “Hello everyone, I’m Pasquale, the gentleman in the video. THANK YOU to everyone for the kind words and for the affection shown .” (Pasquale has his own Instagram account . The description on his channel, translated from Italian, reads: “Music is part of my lifestyle; it thrills me, gives me strength, moves me… stimulates me.”) View this post on Instagram Someone else in the comments shared that Pasquale does a group dance class at the local senior center. What a wonderful way to stay vital and healthy in your golden years. (And for anyone wondering the status of the “couple,” someone else said they’re just friends.) Sometimes you just have to put some music and dance in the piazza, just for the fun of it. This article originally appeared in August. It has been updated. items.descriptionOriginal: When hundreds of Polish children arrived in India’s Nawanagar state (now Jamnagar, in Gujarat) during World War II , they had already been driven from their homes, survived Soviet labor camps, and lived through years of uncertainty . The war had stripped away school, friends, and the everyday routines most children naturally build their lives around. According to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum , the children’s journey had begun years earlier. Following the Soviet invasion of eastern Poland in 1939, about half a million Polish civilians were deported to labor camps in Siberia and Kazakhstan. After the 1941 Sikorski-Mayski Agreement allowed many Polish civilians to leave the Soviet Union, some eventually made the long journey through Iran to India. A portrait of Maharaja Jam Saheb Digvijaysinhji Ranjitsinhji Jadeja, 1935. Photo credit: Bassano LTD/ Wikimedia Commons Creating a space to just be a kid again A July 2026 Smithsonian Magazine story recounts how Maharaja Digvijaysinhji Ranjitsinhji Jadeja, the ruler of one of India’s princely states, Nawanagar, welcomed those children and created far more than a temporary refuge to wait out the war. Instead, he built a community where everyday life could begin again. There in Balachadi, nearly 1,000 children between the ages of 2 and 15 were given a safe place to stay from 1942 to 1946. A special camp was constructed near the maharaja’s summer palace on the Kathiawar Peninsula. The settlement included barracks, a school, a library, a Catholic church, kitchens, and places to play. The children returned to the classroom where Polish teachers continued lessons in their native language. Religious services and holidays like Christmas were observed much as they had before the war. Alongside food and shelter, the camp preserved familiar routines that helped restore a sense of normal life. Instead of wondering where they would sleep or where their next meal would come from, they worried about homework or raced across playing fields with new friends. He treated the children as his own children Wieslaw Stypula was only 11 years old when he joined the Balachadi community in 1942. In the 2013 documentary A Little Poland in India , Stypula recounted, “In this very grim scenario, I was adopted by people of a country I did not even know. It was here that I found happiness.” Digvijaysinhji called the children his own children. He would welcome new groups of Polish children, saying, “Do not consider yourself orphans any more. You are now Nawanagaris, and I am Bapu, father of all the people of Nawanagar, so also yours.” He was also dedicated to honoring their Polish identity. Anu Radha ,the filmmaker behind the documentary, told Smithsonian , “He insisted that every day, the Polish flag should be hoisted in the camp, and all children sing the Polish national anthem, in spite of the fatherland not being free.” The maharaja with kids and women from Poland. Alewis2388/ Wikimedia Commons Remarkable instincts without the modern humanitarian handbook Today, global relief organizations like UNICEF emphasize that children displaced by war need more than food and shelter . Education, opportunities to play, and cultural identity are all important parts of helping children recover from traumatic experiences. These ideas are reflected in UNICEF’s child-friendly spaces, which let children play, continue learning, and begin healing from trauma. They also echo a June 2026 statement from Save the Children for the International Day of Play, which says a safe place to play allows a child in conflict “to still hold on to part of their childhood.” For the children who arrived in Balachadi more than 80 years ago, the community the maharaja fostered became more than a refuge. It gave them the chance to be children again. The maharaja has not been forgotten. Warsaw has a Good Maharaja Square and schools named in his honor, and Poland posthumously awarded him the Commander’s Cross of the Order of Merit in 2011. When Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited Warsaw in 2024, he paid tribute at a memorial to the maharaja and announced a youth exchange program named for the Jam Saheb, whose first group of 21 Polish youths later visited Jamnagar. This article originally appeared in August. It has been updated. The post A rich maharaja took in 1,000 Polish kids during WWII, recreating their home on Indian soil appeared first on Upworthy .

items.description: Θα πίστευε κανείς ότι οι πολύ έξυπνοι άνθρωποι έχουν ευκολότερη ζωή. Όλη αυτή η εγκεφαλική δύναμη θα πρέπει να κάνει κάποιον πιο πειθαρχημένο, καλύτερο στη λήψη αποφάσεων και πιο επικεντρωμένο στη φροντίδα της ψυχικής του υγείας. Ωστόσο, το να έχεις έναν υπερδύναμο εγκέφαλο έρχεται με τα δικά του προβλήματα, όπως το να έχεις μια Ferrari θα σου φέρει περισσότερη θλίψη από το να έχεις ένα Toyot…
items.descriptionOriginal: One would think that highly intelligent people have easier lives. All that brainpower should make someone more disciplined, better at decision-making, and more focused on taking good care of their mental health. However, having a super-powered brain comes with its own problems, much like owning a Ferrari will give you more grief than owning a Toyota. Some people may be super smart but don’t really believe it because their lives aren’t exactly perfect and they still struggle with their faults and foibles. But that just means they’re human. In fact, highly intelligent people face challenges that aren’t necessarily solved by simply thinking their way out of them. Three ‘bad habits’ that super smart people often have Some research has linked these habits (that some folks deem “bad”) to higher scores on certain tests of ability. That doesn’t prove you’re highly intelligent, but it’s a good reason to go easy on yourself. 1. Smart people get bored easily Some researchers and educators have suggested that highly intelligent people get bored when forced to pFerform repetitive tasks or when activities are too easy. The evidence is mixed, though. A 2022 study of nearly 2,900 German third graders found that general cognitive ability was barely related to boredom, and that how interested students were in a subject mattered far more. However, there is some good news. People who enjoy thinking tend to seek out intellectual stimulation, which can help them find something interesting in a tedious task. Two students looking bored. Photo credit: Canva 2. Smart people swear a lot People often chastise those who use bad words for having a small vocabulary, which forces them to resort to vulgar language rather than find a more elegant way to express themselves. However, a 2015 study in Language Sciences found that people who could name more swear words in a minute also tended to name more non-swear words, which suggests that swearing fluency goes along with verbal fluency rather than a limited vocabulary. So, next time someone gives you grief for using colorful language, you can point out that it doesn’t mean you’re short on words. 3. Smart people stay up late A 2024 study from Imperial College London found that night owls, those who go to bed late, and early risers, those who get up early, scored differently on cognitive tests. The study drew on data from more than 26,000 UK Biobank participants. In two separate tests, night owls scored 13.5% and 7.5% higher than early risers. Those in the middle or “intermediate” types also scored higher than the early risers, by 10.6% and 6.3%. Why night owls may have an edge Night owls are often seen as lazy or undisciplined, so it may surprise some people that they scored higher on cognitive tests than those who go to bed early. The researchers noted that the study shows an association, not a cause, and that sleeping seven to nine hours a night was linked to the best brain function overall. It seems that at least part of the old adage, “Early to bed and early to rise makes a man healthy, wealthy, and wise,” may not hold up. That doesn’t mean morning people are out of luck, though. The researchers noted that not all early risers perform worse. So, what does it all add up to? Ultimately, it seems that our assumptions about smart people aren’t all true. Many enjoy salty language, stay up late at night, and have a hard time paying attention if they aren’t being challenged. It goes to show that even though intelligence is a blessing, it doesn’t lead to a life that always looks perfect from the outside. And that if you struggle with staying focused, minding your language, or binge-watching late-night TV, it doesn’t mean you aren’t smart; in fact, it could be the exact opposite. This article originally appeared in July. It has been updated. The post If you have any of these 3 ‘bad habits,’ it could mean you’re highly intelligent appeared first on Upworthy .

Υπάρχουν οι διάλεκτοι της Νέας Αγγλίας, με πιο γνωστή την προφορά της Βοστώνης: Pahk the cah στο Havahd yahd! Η προφορά της Νέας Υόρκης είναι παγκοσμίως γνωστή…
items.descriptionOriginal: American English comes in all sorts of different flavors and varieties. I grew up in Baltimore, which shares some dialectical DNA with the accent you find in other Northeastern cities like Philadelphia. Baldamor, hon! There are the New England dialects, most famously the Boston accent : Pahk the cah at Havahd yahd! The New York accent is world famous, as is the deep Southern twang, which gives way to a thick Cajun accent the closer you get to the bayous of Louisiana. These are all different versions of the greater American dialect . But there is one place, a tiny island off the coast of North Carolina, where a few residents speak in such a unique way that many listeners don’t even recognize it as American. Ocracoke, North Carolina, is home to a unique dialect called the Brogue, a blend of American Southern and English, Irish and Scottish influences from the 1600s. The Brogue, also known as Hoi Toider, is absolutely fascinating to hear in action. When you watch interviews with the locals of the island, they at first appear to be speaking a form of deep American Southern, and you can hear the twang the way you might in parts of Georgia or Alabama. But then, without warning, a word or phrase will slip out that sounds distinctly British. Centuries-old English, even. Then you’ll swear you hear a bit of Irish! How the Brogue took shape The dialect owes its roots to a surprising source: Pirates. Pirates loved to hide out on Ocracoke because the island is incredibly remote, roughly 20 miles from the mainland of North Carolina. Even today there are no bridges to Ocracoke and no scheduled commercial flights. Most visitors arrive by ferry, and some by private plane. Eventually, the island was purchased by William Howard, a man said to have served as Blackbeard’s quartermaster (yes, that Blackbeard), and his family helped build the settlement that followed. English sailors and Native American tribes also passed through and had their own unique impact on the culture and developing language of the island. In case you have your doubts about the island’s buccaneerish roots, there’s a popular legend about its name: “In one popular island legend, Ocracoke comes from the phrase, ‘Oh, crow cock,’ which was spoken by the infamous pirate Blackbeard as he waited to do battle at sunrise with the governor’s forces that had come to capture him,” writes a guide from NC State University. The dialect had a lot of room to develop without much outside influence. The BBC writes, “Howard’s community lived in near-isolation for almost two centuries. Electricity didn’t arrive at the island until 1938 and a ferry service didn’t start until 1957, leaving the islanders cut off except for the occasional supply trip to the mainland.” Words only locals would know That’s why Hoi Toider is still alive to this day, although its speaking population has dwindled to a few hundred people at most. Here are a few hallmark phrases of the unique dialect: A “dingbatter” is anyone not from the island, such as a tourist. An “O’cocker” is a native islander. “Meehonkey” is the island word for hide-and-seek. The Brogue uses ‘weren’t’ liberally for singular nouns (“The sun weren’t out yesterday.”) and frequently adds an ‘a’ in front of verbs (“We went a-fishin’ this morning”). But to fully appreciate Hoi Toider, you’ve got to hear it in action: Why the Brogue is slowly fading Experts say, as awesome as the Brogue is, it will likely disappear within the next 50 years. Though the island remains about as remote as it comes, there’s no escaping the influence of social media, television, and film these days. Every generation born on the island is a smidge less likely to adopt the Brogue than the one that came before. It will probably be mostly gone in the next couple of generations, which feels like a tragedy. Instead of “dingbatter” and “meehonkey,” the kids will be saying “rizz” and “no cap.” OK, maybe that’s an exaggeration, but young people growing up on the island won’t be as immersed in the language as their elders and will begin to speak more and more like your average American. There’s a concept called cultural homogenization . It’s the idea that over time, because of technology and globalization, unique individual cultures from around the world will all start to look more and more the same. It’s why you see fast food chains in the shadow of historic landmarks and people all over the globe listening to the same handful of musical artists. Ocracoke has managed to hang on longer than most places due to how difficult it is to reach. Here’s hoping that the Ocracoke Brogue can survive somehow, some way, in little pockets of the island. It’s just too dang cool and interesting to go away just yet. This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post The remote island where residents speak a fascinating blend of Southern and Old English appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Endangered Animals Making a Comeback in 2027 Reading Time: 4 minutes Endangered Animals Making a Comeback in 2027 When you hear about endangered wildlife, it’s often another story of shrinking habitats, declining populations or species facing extinction. However, there is good news worth celebrating, too. Thanks to dedicated conservation efforts, some of the world’s most threatened animals are making remarkable comebacks. From mountain gorillas thriving in protected forests to bald eagles soaring across North America, you’ll find encouraging examples of how conservation can reverse population declines. Discover inspiring wildlife recovery stories that offer hope to endangered animals and show how your support for conservation can make a difference. 1. Mountain Gorillas Decades of habitat protection, veterinary care and anti-poaching initiatives have helped mountain gorilla populations grow to over 1,000 individuals , with multiple family groups. It’s a significant improvement for a species that once faced a much bleaker future. You’ll find these great apes in two isolated regions of Central and East Africa, where conservation teams work alongside local communities to protect the remaining habitat. The survival of this primate species extends beyond the gorillas themselves. Protecting large primates can also preserve entire ecosystems. While mountain gorillas remain endangered, their growing numbers demonstrate the value of long-term conservation. Expanding these efforts to other primate species may also protect smaller endangered species. 2. Bald Eagles Few wildlife recoveries are as impressive as that of the bald eagle. Once threatened by hunting, habitat destruction and the irresponsible use of the pesticide commonly known as DDT, America’s national bird has made an extraordinary species comeback. DDT led to poor-quality egg production, making successful breeding incredibly difficult for bald eagles. The ban on DDT, stronger legal protections and habitat conservation helped reverse decades of population decline. According to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, the population in the lower 48 states increased from approximately 72,434 birds in 2009 to just over 316,000 birds , with 71,467 breeding pairs tracked between 2018 and 2019. Today, you’ll see bald eagles near rivers, lakes and coastlines across much of North America. Their remarkable recovery shows how environmental laws and sustained conservation efforts can give threatened wildlife a second chance. 3. Sea Turtles For sea turtles, the journey to adulthood begins with a dangerous dash from nest to ocean. Fortunately, conservation programs are giving more hatchlings a fighting chance through beach patrols, nest monitoring and community involvement. In the Philippines, conservationists have even recruited four-legged helpers. Project CURMA’s Paw Patrol uses specially trained dogs to sniff out buried turtle eggs , allowing volunteers to locate and protect nests from poachers and other threats. Efforts to reduce accidental catches in fishing nets, restore nesting beaches and limit artificial lighting along the coastlines are helping protect sea turtles at different stages of their lives. Some populations have shown encouraging improvements following decades of protection. While several sea turtle species remain endangered or critically endangered, initiatives like these show that creative conservation strategies can improve their chances of survival. When you participate in community initiatives, such as Paw Patrol, you increase the support that struggling species need to survive. 4. Tigers Tigers have lost much of their historical range to deforestation, human development and poaching. However, conservation efforts in parts of Asia are helping these magnificent predators reclaim lost ground. Wild tigers live across parts of Asia, where conservation efforts have helped some populations rebound after the global population fell to an estimated 3,200 in 2010. India offers one of the strongest examples, as it is now home to about 70% of the world’s wild tigers. Forest conservation has played a valuable part in this and other success stories. Sustainable forestry and other interventions have slowed global deforestation rates by almost 40% since the 1990s, which is why purchasing sustainably sourced timber is so important, whether you buy new floors, furniture or even musical instruments. Habitat loss remains a threat, but support for responsible forest management offers hope. 5. American Alligators American alligators were once hunted so extensively for their valuable skins that their survival became a serious concern. By 1967, the species had gained federal endangered status, prompting stronger protections against hunting and illegal trade. Conservation measures, including regulated harvesting and wetland management, helped restore their numbers. The species was removed from the U.S. endangered species list in 1987, just two decades after receiving protection. Today, up to 1.06 million mature American alligators inhabit the southeastern United States. With the species now classified as least concern, you’re looking at one of America’s most successful wildlife recovery stories. 6. Other Stories of Recovery The good news continues across the world. Other threatened species are showing encouraging signs of recovery, giving you even more reasons to feel hopeful about wildlife conservation. The Iberian lynx has rebounded from near extinction, thanks to captive breeding and habitat restoration across Spain and Portugal. North Atlantic right whales are also showing tentative signs of population growth, although their survival remains precarious. Meanwhile, giant pandas have benefited from decades of habitat protection and breeding programs, while southern white rhinos have recovered significantly from historical population lows through intensive conservation efforts. Humpback whales offer another success story, with several populations rebounding after commercial whaling restrictions gave these ocean giants a chance to recover. These achievements highlight the importance of patience and persistence, as rebuilding wildlife populations often requires decades of protection and ongoing monitoring. Every contribution makes a difference, and even keeping your distance from these animals, respecting protected habitats and choosing ethical wildlife tourism experiences contribute to various species’ success stories. Why Are More Endangered Animals Recovering? Wildlife recovery rarely happens by chance. Behind these success stories are years of coordinated conservation efforts, scientific research and communities working to protect vulnerable species. These efforts also benefit entire ecosystems. When you protect forests, wetlands and oceans, you’re helping preserve the habitats that countless species depend on for survival. Several approaches are helping endangered animals rebuild their populations: Habitat protection: National parks, wildlife corridors and sustainable land management give animals safer places to live, breed and find food. Stronger wildlife laws: Hunting restrictions, anti-poaching patrols and international trade regulations help reduce human-driven threats. Breeding and reintroduction programs: Conservationists can raise threatened animals in protected environments and then release them into suitable habitats where they have a better chance of thriving. Community involvement: Local conservation projects encourage people to protect wildlife while supporting livelihoods through responsible tourism and sustainable practices. Scientific monitoring: Tools like GPS collars, population surveys, and genetic research help conservationists spot problems earlier and celebrate progress when recovery efforts work. A Brighter Future for Endangered Wildlife Every species making a comeback represents years of dedication and a reminder that extinction isn’t always inevitable. Although many endangered animals still face serious threats, these conservation successes show that meaningful progress is possible. You can help sustain that momentum by supporting wildlife conservation organizations, choosing responsibly sourced products and spreading awareness about threatened species. Even small actions contribute to a broader movement to protect biodiversity. With continued commitment, today’s recovery stories could become tomorrow’s thriving wildlife populations. The post Endangered Animals Making a Comeback in 2027 appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: A former Los Angeles gang member, a former skinhead and a former radical Islamist walk into a youth center. What sounds like the setup for an uneasy joke is at the core of Farah Pandith’s work: Put people who might otherwise never share a room in front of young people; let them explain what drew them into extremism and how they found their way out. “They’re the most authentic and credible voices there are,” Pandith says. More than once she has observed that their stories reach an audience that official warnings cannot. For decades, including while working for the U.S. government under the Obama, George W. Bush and George H.W. Bush administrations, Pandith researched why people embrace ideologies that divide the world into “us versus them.” Before people can be persuaded away from hatred, she argues, one has to understand what they are looking for: recognition, certainty or a place in the world. “You don’t suddenly explode and become an extremist overnight. You’re having some self-doubt, you’re asking questions about who you are,” she says from her light-filled living room in Arlington, Virginia. Preventing someone from becoming an extremist has been her lifelong goal, because it’s “infinitely easier than dealing with the fallout.” Farah Pandith visits the Indonesian city of Bekasi during her time as the U.S. special representative to Muslim communities. Credit: U.S. Embassy, Jakarta / Wikimedia Commons While working for the government, she traveled to nearly 100 countries, from Belgium to Bangladesh, to understand how extremists’ descent into violence can be interrupted. Today she applies what she learned to a broader problem: how to make compassion more than an admirable sentiment and help communities put it into practice. Last year Pandith received the ADL Daniel Pearl Award , which is given annually to a person who has had a positive impact on understanding between Jews and the Muslim world, and is sponsored by the parents of the journalist who was kidnapped and killed in Pakistan in 2002. “It is hard to think of anyone more knowledgeable than Farah Pandith when it comes to countering violent extremism,” Joseph Nye, the late chair of the National Intelligence Council, said about her. On September 11, 2001, Pandith watched on television like millions of others as two planes struck the World Trade Center. “It felt very heavy,” she recalls, putting a hand to her heart. “The world kind of went still for a moment, like, ‘What do we do about this?’” She felt compelled to act, to help prevent such violence from happening again. She especially rejected the way extremists attempted to define her religion on the airwaves. “Who are they to dictate what Islam is?” she remembers thinking. “For me, Islam means humility, compassion, to treat others with respect.” Initially, when she worked for the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), cooperating with local organizations showed her that effective policy depends on understanding the people on the ground. “You have to listen really well to find a solution that matches with the local community,” she says. “That’s tricky and complex. Trust has to be built first.” The same principle, she realized, applied to preventing violent extremism. Government officials could not design effective strategies from Washington alone. They needed to hear from the people they hoped to reach, including those whose voices had been overlooked. After joining the National Security Council in 2004, Pandith helped develop the “soft power” side of the Global War on Terror through a new approach called Countering Violent Extremism. Military action might disrupt extremist organizations, but it could not prevent them from recruiting new members. Nor were public relations campaigns successful in overcoming the distrust of Muslims worldwide. Even in her own government, distrust was impossible to ignore. One congressman called the White House to complain a “jihadist” was sitting in the Council. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Pandith was briefly living in Afghanistan’s capital, Kabul, in 2004 when photographs of abuse at Abu Ghraib surfaced showing American soldiers humiliating Muslim prisoners. “In an instant, all our efforts on the ground were harmed irreparably,” she says. Locals asked how she could represent a government that treated Muslim prisoners that way. The experience reinforced a lesson: Building trust also meant receiving criticism, sitting through uncomfortable conversations. Pandith carried that approach into her work at the State Department, where Hillary Clinton appointed her the first U.S. special representative to Muslim communities in 2009. Instead of treating Muslim populations as a single audience for American messages, she traveled widely, meeting people in homes, mosques and community settings to learn what mattered to them. “You have to go to the rural areas,” she says, aiming to support credible local voices that could offer alternatives to extremist narratives. Pandith herself has been shaped by a background that made her an ideal diplomat. She came to the U.S. from Kashmir as a baby with her mother, a pulmonologist and the medical director of a hospital. Pandith describes growing up in a highly educated Muslim family without experiencing discrimination. She remembers an America in which people of different faiths could live alongside one another, “with a synagogue, a church, a mosque and a temple in the same part of town.” Today, she admits, that harmonious coexistence feels nearly impossible. Her parents separated when she was 10, and her mother raised Pandith and her brother on her own. One of her greatest influences was her uncle, a heart surgeon. “I’ve held the hearts of different people in my hands,” he would tell her. “Always remember: There is no difference between the heart of a Muslim, a Jew, a Hindu or a Christian.” Pandith feels she carries “many identities” — an American, a woman, a Muslim and a foreign policy professional, among others. While traveling as Special Representative to Muslim Communities in the Obama administration, she said she had a “superpower” when speaking with Muslims. When she told them she was born in Srinagar in Kashmir, India, the atmosphere often changed. “Suddenly I’m like a sister to them.” Farah Pandith on a panel at the Milken Institute Asia Summit. Courtesy of Farah Pandith Her ability to forge connections would become one of her greatest professional assets. By chance, Barbara Bush, the wife of President George H.W. Bush, visited Smith College during Farah’s senior year. She was so impressed by a speech Pandith gave as student body president that she helped her secure her job at USAID after graduation. That was how the young woman began traveling around the world. Pandith’s work challenged conventional explanations of radicalization. Poverty and lack of education, she argued, could not explain why people embraced violent ideologies. Some of the 9/11 terrorists were well educated. Pandith pointed to a different cause she observed in Muslim communities: deep identity crises among young people who struggled to find their place in a rapidly changing world. She thinks of a young woman in Denmark whose Imam told her she wasn’t a Muslim if she didn’t cover her head. Or Mubin Shaikh in Canada, who went to Pakistan and Syria as a 19-year-old to fight alongside the jihadists and who now teaches security politics at the University of Ottawa. Pandith has seen firsthand that dialogue can change minds. ““It’s less interesting for the media than an extremist’s video, but the conversations we had affected people.” Her initiatives have sought to make dialogue a shared responsibility. Against Violent Extremism became the world’s first and only network of former extremists, launched by the U.S. Department of State, the Institute for Strategic Dialogue and Google. The “Hours Against Hate” campaign encouraged teenagers to spend an hour doing something for someone different from themselves. Millions participated. Sisters Against Violent Extremism connected mothers concerned about their children’s vulnerability to extremist recruitment. In a citizen-dialogue program, Pandith traveled through Europe with other Muslim Americans to share experiences and listen to local concerns. People had the chance to meet someone they might otherwise see only through stereotypes and to develop a relationship that complicated those assumptions. In her book How We Win , recently reissued, Pandith remains stubbornly optimistic: The fight against extremism can be won. Preventing people from being drawn into extremist movements requires intervening early and bringing together the people who can reach them — not just government officials, but business leaders, teachers, local communities and influencers whose networks, knowledge and credibility government agencies lack. “The fight against violent extremism is not going to be won solely by the efforts of government,” she argues. “We need businesses to step up as never before, for the public interest as well as their own.” She insists that this work cannot be dismissed as idealism or do-goodery but is “a matter of national security” — as important as the hard power of military force. Pandith emphasizes that the underlying lessons can be relevant for many communities. The same dynamics of exclusion and dehumanization can fuel hostility toward religious minorities, LGBTQ+ people and Asian communities, among others. Still, she admits that the strategies for countering violent extremism never fully came to fruition, often mired in bureaucracy. “Congress provided just 0.0138 percent of funding compared to the funding for the military,” she calculates. “We know what we need to do. We spent 25 years researching and exchanging strategies. But we left the field to the extremists.” Pandith sees the reality as a call to action: “We cannot just wring our hands and keep saying things are bad and things are difficult and somebody else’s problem. We need everybody.” Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime She now works outside government to advance another part of this agenda, as senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations , teaching countering violent extremism at Georgetown University, and as a Global Peace Laureate for the Muhammad Ali Center. She has been developing the Muhammad Ali Index on compassion . For Pandith, compassion is the capacity to recognize another person’s humanity even amid disagreement, and to resist the impulse to turn differences into a reason for contempt. “There isn’t a faith on planet Earth that doesn’t have compassion in it. And even if you are not religious you understand what it means, right?” As part of the Muhammed Ali Index, more than 5,400 people in 12 American cities responded to the 2025 State of Compassion survey . Sixty-one percent said they felt compassion has declined in the last four years, but 43 percent were optimistic about the future of compassion in America. A second index, planned for 2027, will cover 20 U.S. cities and 12 cities around the world. The ambition is practical. Pandith hopes the data will help mayors, school leaders, faith groups and local organizations identify opportunities to build stronger connections and design efforts suited to their own communities. The point is not to prescribe a universal program, but to create a framework that can be adapted. “We want to see people taking inspiration from the data to actually do something over time so we can measure and see what takes place,” she says passionately, insisting that compassion can be trained: “Compassion is a muscle that can be exercised.” Yet the starting point is personal: “Self-compassion is essential.” Building the capacity for compassion, Pandith argues, begins with recognizing what is happening inside oneself. She is particularly interested in reaching young people early. “The world that they are growing up in is so polarized and so difficult and so different from the one that we have grown up in,” she says, “that they don’t have a memory of people who are different from them speaking to each other with dignity regularly.” As Pandith sees it, waiting for polarization to disappear on its own is not a strategy. The task is to build relationships and connections that open up hearts and minds — and to keep investing in them long enough to learn what works. She repeats her favorite sentence: “Solutions are available and affordable.” UPDATE — November 3, 2026: This story has been updated to clarify facts about Pandith’s work and background. items.titleOriginal: ‘The Sky Had No Stars’: Gurugram Student Builds Free Website To Check Light Pollution Using a Phone Photo

Σε μια πόλη όπου ο νυχτερινός ουρανός σπάνια προσφέρει καθαρή θέα στα αστέρια, ακόμη και μια χούφτα μπορεί να μετατρέψει μια συνηθισμένη βραδιά σε…
items.descriptionOriginal: When Suhani Gupta and her sister spot more than seven stars from their balcony in Gurugram, they have a reason to celebrate. They step outside, open Stellarium, an astronomy app, and try to identify the constellations above them. In a city where the night sky rarely offers a clear view of the stars, even a handful can turn an ordinary evening into an occasion. "My sister and I get excited when we see more than seven stars in the sky," Suhani tells The Better India. The sisters initially assumed that air pollution was responsible for the limited visibility. After all, Gurugram frequently experiences haze. But visits to her grandparents in Udhampur, Jammu and Kashmir , offered Suhani a different perspective. The sky there appeared far more generous with stars. The stars had not suddenly multiplied in the mountains. Something about the surroundings had changed. That difference led Suhani to investigate light pollution — the excessive or poorly directed use of artificial light that brightens the night sky and makes celestial objects harder to see. Buildings, roads, commercial establishments and other sources of outdoor lighting can contribute to this glow. The consequences extend beyond astronomy, affecting nocturnal wildlife, ecosystems and human exposure to darkness. Unlike a polluted river or a visible plume of smoke, an increasingly bright night sky can be difficult to recognise as an environmental change. Photograph: (Alexey Elfimov) But how could a school student measure a problem that even many adults rarely recognise? In May 2025, Suhani, now a Class 12 student, began teaching herself image processing and developing SkyQi, a free online platform that estimates night-sky quality using photographs taken on smartphones . The project has since grown into a citizen-science initiative, attracting observations from users across dozens of countries. In 2026, she took the investigation further. Using NASA satellite data, she examined changes in night-time radiance across 50 Indian cities between 2015 and 2025. Her analysis found that the median city's measured night-time radiance was 70% higher in 2025 than in 2015, while 47 of the 50 cities recorded an increase. Leh, known for its dark skies and astronomy tourism, showed the steepest rise in her dataset, at 546%. The findings do not directly measure how bright the sky appears to someone standing on the ground. They do, however, raise questions about how urban growth, tourism and outdoor lighting are changing India's nights. For Suhani, the aim is to make those changes easier to observe, understand and eventually address. From a school astronomy club to a pollution problem Suhani's interest in light pollution began in 2024, when she was part of her school's space society. During meteor showers and other astronomical events, members would gather on voice chat at around 3 am to watch the sky. Observing the stars required patience. Participants would spend about 30 minutes outside, allowing their eyes to adjust to the darkness before attempting to identify celestial objects. "While we generally do that to adjust to the moon's brightness, the haze in our sky was much more, and that is kind of how I got into light pollution," she explains. She began watching YouTube videos and reading research on the effects of artificial light on human health, wildlife, ecosystems and astronomy. Suhani had previously worked with Arduinos and Raspberry Pi and built a visual aid for people who are blind using vision-language models and computer vision. Photograph: (Suhani Gupta; Getty Images) "Unlike other forms of pollution, air, water, or even noise, light pollution came on gradually, so we never even knew it was taking over our skies," she says. Unlike a polluted river or a visible plume of smoke, an increasingly bright night sky can be difficult to recognise as an environmental change. New buildings, illuminated advertisements, streetlights and commercial spaces may appear to make a city safer or more developed. Yet the cumulative effect of unnecessary or poorly directed lighting can reduce the darkness that once allowed people to see the stars. Suhani wanted to understand how this gradual change could be measured. She also wanted to find a method that did not require expensive equipment or specialised astronomical knowledge. Can a smartphone measure the night sky? Professional astronomers use instruments called Sky Quality Meters to measure the brightness of the night sky. These devices provide numerical readings that help observers assess how dark a location is. However, their cost can put them beyond the reach of students, amateur astronomers and community groups. Suhani began exploring whether an ordinary smartphone camera could offer an alternative. She was not entirely new to technology. She had previously worked with Arduinos and Raspberry Pi and built a visual aid for people who are blind using vision-language models and computer vision. Her parents helped her develop the skills required for the project. Both are software engineers from BITS Pilani, and her mother had worked on image processing for Nokia phones. "My mom taught me the concepts, and a lot more Python along the way," Suhani says. She reworked the platform to assess three indicators: the number of visible stars, the difference in brightness between the horizon and the sky directly overhead, and the calculated brightness of the sky. She supplemented these lessons with research papers, programming libraries and help from her father. She also used AI as a learning aid while trying to understand the techniques astronomers use to assess the night sky, including the Bortle scale. The Bortle scale classifies night skies according to their darkness and the visibility of stars and other celestial objects. At one end are heavily light-polluted urban skies; at the other are exceptionally dark skies where the Milky Way and faint celestial objects are visible. Suhani began developing SkyQi in May 2025. The first version assessed a photograph's overall brightness and converted it into a score. But the results were unreliable. A cloudy sky could be mistaken for a light-polluted one. A camera sensor could count bright pixels as stars, while overexposed photographs could distort the readings. "I realised that one measurement wasn't enough," she says. She reworked the platform to assess three indicators: the number of visible stars, the difference in brightness between the horizon and the sky directly overhead, and the calculated brightness of the sky. The platform compares these measurements to determine whether they broadly agree. If they do, it assigns a confidence level to the reading. If they do not, the result can be flagged as less reliable. SkyQi went live in September 2025. However, making the platform available was only the beginning. Suhani soon found that its formula classified too many photographs, including some taken in towns, as almost perfectly dark because the calculation had reached its measurement ceiling. She revised the method to account for information recorded by smartphone cameras, particularly shutter speed and ISO settings. "Two phones can photograph the same sky and produce very different-looking pictures, and a longer exposure makes the sky look brighter, so knowing the settings lets me correct for that," she explains. When these details are missing, as can happen when photographs are forwarded through WhatsApp or edited, SkyQi uses a published world atlas of light pollution as a starting point and adjusts the estimate using information from the photograph. It labels such results as 'Estimated'. The platform also checks cloud forecasts for the location and flags observations that may have been affected by clouds. The system is still evolving. SkyQi currently uses a shared calibration across phone models, while model-specific calibration remains part of Suhani's plans. What makes a reading reliable? Clouds can obscure stars while reflecting artificial light towards the ground. Moonlight can brighten the sky, while camera movement can blur stars or make them difficult to identify. Smartphone image processing can further alter the apparent brightness of a photograph. So SkyQi does not rely on a single indicator. It compares the three measurements and assigns high, medium or low confidence according to how consistently they point towards the same conclusion. A high-confidence reading does not guarantee that the result is correct. It means that the available indicators agree with one another. Suhani has tested an earlier version of the platform against 104 reference night-sky images with known Bortle classifications. According to her, SkyQi's result was within one Bortle class of the reference approximately 65% of the time. However, the tool has not yet been validated against a professional Sky Quality Meter. "I do not possess a professional sky quality meter but one that I made by myself using an Arduino. Thus, I haven't compared it yet with a professional Sky Quality Meter," she tells The Better India. A few hundred photographs containing complete camera settings have been submitted since September, and Suhani hopes to use these observations to improve the platform's calibration. For now, she describes SkyQi as a citizen-science tool rather than a substitute for professional instruments. Its value lies partly in helping people collect observations from different locations and, ideally, repeat them over time. She recommends photographing the sky on clear nights, preferably when the Moon is not visible and at least an hour and a half after sunset. Users should move away from direct light sources, keep their phones steady, point towards an open sky and upload original, unedited photographs. What did 50 Indian cities reveal? Once SkyQi was underway, Suhani turned to a larger question: had India's night skies become brighter over the previous decade? In 2026, she analysed NASA satellite data covering 50 Indian cities in 2015, 2020 and 2025. Her report found that the median city's measured night-time radiance was 70% higher in 2025 than in 2015. Forty-seven cities recorded an increase over the period. Leh stood out, with satellite-observed night-time radiance rising by 546%, according to her analysis. "Leh is one of the only dark sky places left in our country, and despite it being such a remote high-altitude place, we observe light pollution levels increasing," she says. The finding raises particular concerns because Leh and the wider Ladakh region are associated with high-altitude landscapes, astronomy and relatively dark skies. Suhani points to urbanisation and the growth of tourism infrastructure as possible contributors to increasing artificial light. Hotels, homestays, restaurants and other facilities have expanded in places that were previously less developed. A few hundred photographs containing complete camera settings have been submitted since September, and Suhani hopes to use these observations to improve the platform's calibration. This creates a paradox. Visitors travel to Ladakh to experience its night sky, but the infrastructure built to accommodate them can introduce additional artificial light. Communities around Hanle, for instance, have developed homestays and astronomy-related tourism, with residents training to welcome visitors as astronomy guides, sometimes known as Astro Ambassadors. Protecting dark skies could therefore be important not only for astronomical research but also for a tourism economy that depends on them. However, the figures require careful interpretation. "The analysis that suggested a 546% increase was in satellite-observed nighttime radiance from 2015 to now, and while satellite radiance is not a direct measure of ground-level sky brightness, the stark increase suggests a drastic increase even in ground-level sky brightness," Suhani says. What's next for Suhani? Suhani has made her report and the underlying city-level dataset publicly available, allowing other researchers and interested readers to examine the figures. According to the latest figures she shared with The Better India, the platform has received 1,198 photographs from more than 490 contributors across 63 countries. "I was initially skeptical of the reach SkyQi would attain and continue to remain amazed at how many people have tried the tool out," she says. India is currently the third-largest source of readings on the platform, after the United States and China. "The ultimate aim of SkyQi has always been to find or build a community of people passionate about light pollution advocacy and spread awareness about it, and it has achieved exactly that," she says. She hopes schools and astronomy clubs will organise night-sky surveys in which students photograph the sky from the same locations month after month. Repeated observations could help participants identify patterns and locations that need more detailed investigation. For now, the project asks people to do something simple: look up, take a photograph and pay attention to what the sky reveals. "Light pollution isn't something we just have to live with," she says. The question that began on a Gurugram balcony has now expanded to 50 Indian cities and a growing international community of observers . What started as an attempt to understand why the stars looked different in Udhampur has become an effort to measure how artificial light is changing the night.

items.descriptionOriginal: Some bees line their nests with soft petals. Some line them with hardened tree sap. Some line them with a thin, flexible film composed of silk and polyester. And this latter group—known as cellophane bees—may hold the key to sustainable, biodegradable plastic, according to a new study. “Nature has already solved a problem that polymer scientists are still working on: a bioplastic that is chemically and physically similar to conventional plastics but doesn’t persist in the environment,” says study team member Jonathan Coote , assistant professor in the Department of Sustainable Biomaterials at Virginia Tech University. Unlike more familiar hive-dwelling honeybees, cellophane bees nest in the soil. Females lay eggs in individual chambers that they line with secretions from a gland on their abdomen. Scientists have known for almost half a century that this lining is composed of silk fibers and a polyester similar to polyethylene—a material that makes up about one-third of human-produced plastics and is the most commonly used plastic for packaging. “Polyethylene-like polyesters made in the lab generally don’t break down well in the environment,” says Coote. “The bees’ material, however, breaks down rapidly in soil.” Although the bees nest in aggregations of 10,000 or more individual nests and often use the same nest sites for decades, their habitat never becomes choked with plastic—in contrast to large aggregations of modern humans. To find out more about how the bees do it, Coote and his collaborators gathered nest linings from two Tennessee nest sites of a species of cellophane bee known as Colletes inaequalis . They put the material through a battery of tests to characterize its structure and chemical makeup. They also collected nest linings that had been in the ground for four, seven, and 11 months to track how the material degrades over time. .IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl , .IRPP_ruby The tradeoff at the heart of bioplastics. A fresh nest cell lining is about 73% polyester and 27% silk by weight, the researchers report. The polyester is semicrystalline, likely has cross-linked polymer chains, and has a crystal structure and degradation temperature similar to that of polyethylene. “The biggest surprise was that the material is most likely cross-linked, meaning its polymer chains are chemically tied together into a network,” says Coote. “Cross-linked plastics, called thermosets, are typically very durable, and designing thermosets that break down at the end of their life is a major challenge in polymer science. So finding a thermoset that breaks down rapidly in soil was very counterintuitive, and it’s exciting to have a natural example to learn from.” By four months, the nest linings are just 40% polyester, meaning that the polyester degrades even more rapidly than famously biodegradable silk in the first months (after that, the composition changes much more slowly). Four-month-old nest linings remain flexible and intact, protecting the nest cell from moisture and microbes like a shrink-wrapped bell pepper at the grocery store. By seven months, about the time the larva has developed into an adult bee, the lining easily cracks easily; by 11 months, it crumbles in the hand. In other words, unlike that bell pepper’s shrink wrap, the nest lining lasts just as long as is needed to protect the developing bee, and no longer. The researchers next aim to investigate how the material breaks down so quickly. They hypothesize that the particularities of polyester’s crystal structure may leave the bonds that connect the material’s subunits exposed to a greater degree than in other polyesters. There’s also evidence of an enzyme that breaks these bonds present in the nest lining, perhaps from the mother bee’s saliva. “The goal is to reverse engineer what the bees are doing so that we can design similar materials in the lab and eventually produce them at practical scale,” Coote says. Source: Coote J.P., et al. “ Rapid soil degradation of a cross-linked, semicrystalline polyethylene-like polyester produced by Colletes bees .” PNAS 2026. Image: Laura Russo.

items.descriptionOriginal: This story is part of "Parenting: What Google Won't Tell You" — The Better India's people-led parenting series that goes beyond conventional advice to document how real families are actually raising their children. Through real parents, parenting coaches, influencers and experts, the series brings honest, diverse and relatable perspectives on the questions, choices, challenges and solutions that shape everyday parenting — the things Google can't always answer. As the evening sky turns dark, little diyas begin to flicker along balconies and windowsills. Inside one Faridabad home, the preparations for Diwali are a little different. Three-year-old Rishaan Garg Batra is getting ready to celebrate with his parents, Neha Garg and Siddhant Batra, and his four furry siblings, the family's dogs. There are diyas to light, a family photograph to take, friends and relatives to meet, games to play and , of course, plenty of good food to look forward to. There is one thing missing from the celebrations, though: firecrackers. There is also no last-minute rush to buy new clothes or festive decorations. Growing up with four furry siblings, three-year-old Rishaan is learning why firecrackers can frighten animals and harm the environment. For Neha, a podcaster, writer and brand strategist, and Siddhant, an IT and sports entrepreneur, Diwali has always been about the simple joys of being together. The couple has never been particularly drawn to loud celebrations or the idea of buying something new for every occasion. Over the years, they have built their own little traditions around the festival of lights, and now they are bringing up Rishaan with the same understanding. For Rishaan, this is what Diwali looks like: a few lights, familiar faces, meals shared with loved ones and memories made together. 2 childhood experiences that changed how they celebrate Diwali Neha and Siddhant had each grown uncomfortable with firecrackers long before becoming parents, though for different reasons. Siddhant's turning point came when his sister spoke to him about child labour associated with the manufacture of firecrackers. The two siblings decided to stop bursting them around Grades 5 or 6. Eventually, the rest of the family also adopted a low-noise Diwali. Neha, on the other hand, grew up in a large joint family where firecrackers were an important part of the festivities. Every year, a huge stock would be purchased and divided among the different family units, with each child receiving their share. But she was never particularly fond of them. "I just didn't like the loudness and the cloud of smoke that is left behind after we burst them," she recalls. Something else stayed with her, too. Her mother suffered from severe allergies because of the smoke. While the rest of the family went upstairs to burst crackers, her mother would often remain in the kitchen, coughing and struggling with the fumes. From reusing festive outfits to skipping unnecessary shopping, Neha and Siddhant are teaching their son that celebrations need not come with new purchases. "Seeing her, I would feel really triggered, and I would always wonder, why are we doing this if this is making her so uncomfortable?" says Neha. Instead of joining the others, she would stay back with her mother and help prepare the elaborate Diwali meal. As they grew older, both began to understand the wider consequences of the practice, from air and noise pollution to the distress it causes animals. Being dog lovers, the latter was particularly difficult for them to overlook. When they eventually came together as a couple, not bursting firecrackers was simply something they agreed on. '90% of our kid's wardrobe is preloved pieces' Another thing that Neha and Siddhant have never associated with festivals is shopping. Despite growing up in very different family settings, both had similar ideas about buying new clothes for special occasions. For Neha, weddings were when new clothes were usually purchased. With several weddings taking place in her extended family, there were always outfits that could be reused for festivals. Siddhant, too, never really understood the idea that every festival had to come with a new wardrobe. In fact, he would find it difficult to relate to school essays that described buying new clothes as an essential part of festive celebrations. Today, the couple follows the same approach at home. "We wear clothes we already own, restyle outfits and avoid shopping simply because a festival is around the corner," says Neha. Lighting diyas together is one of the family's favourite Diwali traditions, bringing everyone together for a moment of prayer. Instead, if they choose to spend on something, it is usually food or an experience they can enjoy with family and friends. "Food is a big, big part of how we celebrate and how we see celebrations and how we see togetherness. And if at all our money goes in anything material, it goes on food," Neha says. The same thinking extends to Rishaan's wardrobe. Since he was born, the couple has consciously encouraged friends and family to give him preloved clothes instead of buying new ones. Today, nearly 90 per cent of his wardrobe consists of preloved pieces, including everyday outfits, party wear and traditional clothes such as kurtas . For Neha and Siddhant, this is not something they practise only during Diwali. It is a lifestyle choice they want their son to grow up considering perfectly normal . Growing up with four furry siblings At home, some of Rishaan's earliest lessons about being mindful come through his relationship with the family's four dogs. The little one knows that firecrackers can frighten his furry siblings and that the smoke and noise affect animals around them. He has also begun understanding why his parents choose not to burst crackers. Siddhant says Rishaan sometimes takes it upon himself to explain this to others. "If he sees people burning crackers, he goes up to them and says that, you know, this is a bad thing. You should not do it; it causes pollution." Food, family games and visits to friends and relatives make up the celebrations in the Garg Batra household, without the noise of firecrackers. The couple makes it a point to explain the reasoning behind their choices rather than simply asking Rishaan to follow certain rules. They talk to him about what happens when people burst firecrackers, why buying things unnecessarily adds to waste, and what they are choosing when they decide to celebrate differently. For them, he must understand the thought behind these decisions. "Kids are not dumb people. They are very intelligent. They understand if you explain to them logically why you're doing what you're doing," Neha says. A family photograph that includes everyone While Neha and Siddhant prefer simple Diwali celebrations, one family tradition has grown more meaningful as their family has grown. One of their favourite rituals is an annual family photograph. It includes the couple, Rishaan, their four dogs and photographs of the three dogs who have passed away. The tradition began quite spontaneously when it was just Neha, Siddhant and their first two dogs, Scotch and Maya. As their family grew, so did the photograph. When one of their dogs passed away, they decided to include his picture in the frame. The tradition has continued ever since. The family's annual Diwali photograph includes Neha, Siddhant, Rishaan and their four dogs, along with pictures of the three pets they have lost. Today, the photograph is a way of bringing the entire family together, including the furry members who are no longer around. Another ritual they have created is lighting diyas together. On Diwali evening, the family gathers around the lights, takes turns praying and then prays together. "We just pray to the light because it is a festival of light. So on that evening, we light diyas and we pray as a family and we pray as individuals to whatever force there might be," Neha shares. The rest of the day is spent visiting friends and relatives, eating good food and playing games such as Tambola, cards and Dumb Charades. There is no elaborate checklist to get through or pressure to make the day look a certain way. Just time spent with people they love. The little traditions they want their son to carry forward Neha says that becoming parents has made Diwali more meaningful for them. Earlier, the couple was happy keeping the festival simple. Now, they want to create memories and traditions that Rishaan can look forward to every year. Living in Faridabad, they are also aware of the pollution that surrounds the festive season. The family hopes to eventually spend Diwali somewhere less polluted and noisy, away from the city's festivities, although they have not managed to put that plan into action yet. When asked what she hopes Rishaan remembers about Diwali when he grows up, Neha doesn't talk about the things they chose to leave out. Instead, she hopes he remembers the happiness, the food, the games, the family photographs and the time spent with friends and loved ones. By explaining the reasons behind their choices, Neha and Siddhant hope Rishaan grows up making mindful decisions of his own. And for parents who might want to make their celebrations more mindful but worry that their children will miss out, she has a thought drawn from her own experience. "Children miss out on only what they know. If they know your way, they will not miss out on any other way." For Neha and Siddhant, the hope is that Rishaan grows up understanding the reasons behind their choices and finding happiness in the traditions they share. For this family, Diwali is about lighting a few diyas , gathering everyone for that much-loved photograph and making sure there is always room at the table for one more. All images courtesy of Neha Garg

items.descriptionOriginal: A money plant is one of the easiest houseplants to grow . It can grow in a glass jar of water, adding a touch of green to a windowsill, desk, or living room. However, yellowing leaves, rotting stems, and slow growth can leave many plant lovers wondering what they are doing wrong. Dipalee Katre, a plant styling enthusiast from New Delhi, shares simple gardening advice on her Instagram page, 'Wabi Sabi with Dipalee' , where she offers tips on growing plants and creating peaceful green spaces at home . View this post on Instagram A post shared by Wabi Sabi with Dipalee | Plant Styling (@dipalee_katre) In one of her videos, she shares three easy tips to help money plants grow better in water. 1. Cut the stem just below a node When taking a cutting from a money plant , pay attention to the node. This is the point on the stem where leaves and roots can appear. She recommends cutting just below a node when preparing a cutting for propagation. Choosing a healthy stem with at least one node gives the cutting a better chance of developing roots and growing into a new plant. 2. Change the water every week Water that sits in a container for too long can accumulate debris and become unsuitable for healthy root growth. Dipalee advises changing the water at least once a week. Fresh water helps keep the roots clean and reduces the build-up of stagnant water. While changing it, check the roots and stems for any signs of rotting. A clean container also helps maintain a healthier growing environment. 3. Add clean stones or pebbles The third tip is to add clean stones or pebbles to the container. These provide support to the cutting, helping it remain upright instead of shifting around in the water. Make sure the stones are clean before adding them. Avoid packing the container too tightly, as the roots need room to grow. With the right cutting, regular water changes, and a little support from pebbles , growing a money plant in water can be an easier way to bring greenery into your home. As Dipalee suggests, try these tips with your own plant and observe how it responds. After all, a few small changes to your gardening routine can make caring for your indoor plants much easier.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Wildlife Conservation Filmmaking Turns Powerful Stories into Real-World Action Reading Time: 3 minutes Wildlife conservation filmmaking connects audiences with wild places and the people protecting them. Wildlife conservation filmmaking gives viewers a reason to care about wild places they may never see in person. Fin and Fur Films , an award-winning production company, builds its work around that idea. Its team focuses on wildlife, adventure, and conservation stories. The company says it is proudest of films that led to real-world conservation impacts. That goal shapes every project. In wildlife conservation filmmaking, a film succeeds when it moves audiences to care, not just when it entertains. Ben Masters, founder and director, started the company in 2012 with a Kickstarter campaign. Kickstarter is an online fundraising platform where many people donate small amounts. That campaign paid for the film Unbranded. Unbranded follows four young cowboys who adopted, trained, and rode a string of wild mustangs 3,000 miles from Mexico to Canada. That is about the distance across the continental United States. The route crossed some of the wildest terrain in the American West. The trip included runaway horses, a sassy donkey, perilous mountain passes, and rodeos. It also brought sickness, injury, and death. The film won the Audience Award at Telluride Mountainfilm and the Hot Docs Film Festival. Unbranded also shines a light on the complex situation facing the country’s wild horses. The adventure holds attention, and the film explains the issue along the way. Wildlife conservation filmmaking often works this way. The River and the Wall takes a similar approach. Five friends travel 1,200 miles from El Paso to the Gulf of Mexico through the unknown wilds of the Texas borderlands. They go by horse, mountain bike, and canoe. That distance equals nearly a full day of nonstop highway driving, but the friends covered it much more slowly. They set out to document the borderlands. They also wanted to explore how a border wall could affect the natural environment. As the wilderness gave way to the more populated Lower Rio Grande Valley, the friends met the human side of the immigration debate. The trip took an emotional turn they had not planned for. Deep in the Heart: A Texas Wildlife Story brings wildlife conservation filmmaking to an entire state. Actor Matthew McConaughey narrates the visually stunning film. It celebrates Texas landscapes and wildlife found nowhere else. Wildlife conservation filmmaking comes to an entire state in Deep in the Heart: A Texas Wildlife Story , narrated by Matthew McConaughey, a visually stunning film celebrating Texas landscapes and wildlife found nowhere else. Photo courtesy of Fin and Fur Films . The film aims to protect the state’s remaining wild places. It shows how water and wildlife depend on each other. It also recognizes Texas’s important role in conservation across the continent. Reach matters in wildlife conservation filmmaking. Fin and Fur Films has shared its work through Netflix, Apple TV, PBS Nature, Prime, National Geographic, and LoveNature. The films have also appeared in large theatrical releases and on international television. Global Wildlife Conservation notes that well-made environmental documentaries can bring people closer to nature and inspire them to protect it. The Fin and Fur Films catalog shows how that works in practice. Each story pairs a real adventure with a real conservation question. Partnerships help wildlife conservation filmmaking go further. The company has worked with American Rivers, The Nature Conservancy, and Texan by Nature. It has also partnered with brands such as H-E-B and YETI. The numbers show how far a small team can stretch. The company has produced five feature films and more than 30 short films. It has worked with more than 40 conservation groups, which is roughly one partner group per film. See also: A Documentary About Overfishing Sparked Blue Marine Foundation’s Ocean Conservation Mission Masters says the crew keeps its roots as river lovers, backcountry horsemen, and field-savvy wildlife biologists. He also stresses that each film is a team effort. Dozens, or even hundreds, of people contribute to each one. Masters credits partners, collaborators, donors, contractors, and the viewers who give their time to watch. That shared support keeps the work going. Audiences are part of the effort, too. Good stories make conservation feel personal. Wildlife conservation filmmaking gives those stories a wide audience. Which wild place would you most like to see protected next? The post How Wildlife Conservation Filmmaking Turns Powerful Stories into Real-World Action appeared first on Happy Eco News .
