items.descriptionOriginal: What spooks you? A mysterious thud downstairs in the middle of the night, spotting a spider on your pillow, and feeling something brush against your leg in the sea are among the top 10 things that make Brits scream, according to a recent survey of 2,000 adults in the U.K. Yet despite being quick to shriek, the nation appears to embrace the fun side of fear, with 84% of respondents saying scary experiences are more likely to end in laughter than panic when shared with others. More than half also confirmed enjoying spooky thrills in a group setting tends to leave them laughing, particularly when watching horror films, riding roller coasters, or braving a haunted attraction. SWNS According to psychologist Kimberley Wilson, there’s a scientific reason these scary experiences can feel surprisingly enjoyable, something she’s dubbed the “Shared Shriek Effect.” “When we watch something scary, our bodies respond as if we’re facing a threat. Our heart rate increases, adrenaline rises, and our attention sharpens,” she told SWNS. “The difference is that our brains know we’re actually safe, which allows us to experience that physical rush as excitement rather than fear.” Wilson added: “When we share that experience with other people, whether we’re jumping, screaming, or laughing together, it can create a genuine sense of connection. The scream itself also helps release the tension that’s been building up, which is why laughter so often follows.” There are benefits beyond the thrill, too, with a quarter saying that being scared offers an escape from everyday life, while 24% see it as a healthy emotional release. Nearly 1 in 5 of those polled also believe it acts as an instant stress reliever. The research was done via OnePoll and commissioned by M&M’s to mark the launch of the candy brand’s new “ Screaming Service ,” encouraging people to swap streaming for screaming this Halloween. “We think Halloween isn’t really about being scared, it’s about screaming together,” said Georgia Woodward, a senior brand manager at M&M’s. “Our ‘Screaming Service’ celebrates those moments across the month of Halloween when everyone jumps at the same scenes, hides behind a cushion, and ends up laughing together about it afterwards.” Top 10 Things That Make Brits Shriek SWNS 1. Someone unexpectedly jumping out at you as a prank 2. Hearing a knock at the window when it’s dark 3. Hearing a mysterious thud downstairs in the night 4. Missing a step at the bottom of the stairs 5. Spotting a spider on your pillow 6. Feeling something brush against your leg in the sea 7. Seeing a mouse dart across a room 8. Being caught off guard by a spooky film twist 9. Someone unexpectedly shouting “boo!” 10. Walking face-first into a cobweb This article was originally written by Zara Zubeidi for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

Τέτοιες λοιμώξεις μπορεί να είναι δύσκολες…
items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers have discovered that vaccinating mouse mothers transfers antibodies that defend vulnerable newborns against Klebsiella pneumoniae . Klebsiella pneumoniae is a dangerous bacterium that kills thousands of infants in low- and middle-income countries each year and is the leading killer of children globally. Such infections can be difficult to treat due to the bacterium’s growing resistance to antibiotics and there is currently no vaccine available to prevent infection. The study in Science Advances points to a promising new strategy for protecting vulnerable infants from the drug-resistant superbug by harnessing maternal immunity. “ Klebsiella pneumoniae is a serious threat to newborns who have not yet developed their own immune defenses,” says the study’s senior author, David A. Rosen, an associate professor of pediatrics and of molecular microbiology at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis. “Our study shows that maternal immunization can effectively bridge that critical window of vulnerability, giving newborns the protection they need right from birth.” K. pneumoniae is a big problem around the world, especially in the hospital where it can cause pneumonia and other infections among adults and children. In low- and middle-income countries, where children often get exposed to the bacterium in their environment, it drives severe bacterial blood infections, known as sepsis. Because K. pneumoniae is increasingly resistant to standard antibiotics, doctors are often left without effective medicines to treat such infections. The Rosen team collaborated with the lab of Drew Schwartz, an assistant professor of pediatrics, to model K. pneumoniae sepsis in newborn mice that mimics the infection seen in children and asked if vaccinating a pregnant mouse would prevent infection in pups. Female mice were immunized at the time of mating and then again once or twice during pregnancy. The vaccine targets two of the most dangerous types of K. pneumoniae —known as K1 and K2—and was developed by Omniose, a St. Louis-based startup. Rosen had previously published findings that show the vaccine is effective in preventing K. pneumoniae infection in adult mice that can progress to life-threatening liver, respiratory tract, bloodstream, and other infections. Two weeks after birth, the young mice were exposed to lethal doses of the bacteria, either the K1 or K2 type. Of the two-week-old mouse pups from unvaccinated mothers, 0% infected with the K1 type and less than 35% with the K2 type survived. In contrast, of the young mice from vaccinated mothers, more than 80% infected with either type survived. Whether the mother received two or three doses of the vaccine did not impact survival. The researchers drew blood weekly from the young mice starting on their day of birth and continuing up to six weeks of life. They also collected breast milk from lactating mice. They found high concentrations of vaccine-specific antibodies in both the milk of vaccinated mothers and their newborn mice over the course of the study. “Mice that were never immunized themselves are highly protected from a lethal infection just from the durable antibodies transferred to them from their mother,” explains first author Paeton Wantuch, a staff scientist in the Rosen lab. The researchers are now testing updated vaccines designed to shield against multiple strains of the superbug found across the globe. “This study presents the first evidence that giving moms a vaccine could be an effective strategy for protecting their babies against these severe infections,” says Rosen. “And it also has established a practical model that we can now use to test therapies and vaccines that will bring us one step closer to human clinical trials with the ultimate goal of impacting global health.” This work was supported by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases of the National Institutes of Health (NIH), the Gates Foundation, and the Washington University Department of Pediatrics. The content is solely the responsibility of the authors and does not necessarily represent the official view of the NIH, the Gates Foundation or other funders. items.descriptionOriginal: Episode Description: A teenager built a supply distribution network where families request what they need without filling out any forms or declaring themselves as someone in need. She also added a program that researches each family’s cultural background and sends handmade crafts alongside the package. That’s Vivian Ho, the first nominated Local Changemaker in The Optimist Daily’s new series. Arielle and Karissa cover ten solutions this week, including six countries that just put a dollar figure on their EV investments, a Columbia University finding on the minimum movement needed to offset a desk job, and what pest experts actually recommend instead of vinegar. If you have questions, comments, feedback, suggestions, or just want to say hi, send a message to: podcast@optimistdaily.com . Want to be part of the Optimism Movement? Become an Emissary . Subscribe to our FREE Daily/Weekly Newsletter and follow us on Instagram , X , and Blue Sky . The Optimist Daily is a project of the World Business Academy. Donate link: https://www.optimistdaily.com/donate-to-support-the-optimist-daily/?lsc=41ef528d Theme and all original music by Marvin Lanes Transcript: Karissa: Hi, everyone. I’m Karissa. Arielle: I’m Arielle. Karissa: And welcome back to The Optimist Daily’s weekly roundup. Arielle: So good to be back this week. It’s feeling very spooky over here. How about you, Karissa? Karissa: Super spooky and Halloweeny as we prepare for the holiday over the weekend, and a time change over in the US. I know over in Amsterdam, you’re already having those darker evenings. Arielle: Yes, we had our time change last weekend, and yeah, it does get dark so early, and it feels quite wintry, but that’s all right. Karissa: Mm-hmm. I miss the sun. I know. Maybe a week of this weather and I’ll be longing for the sun, but there is no shortage of good news to brighten your day at The Optimist Daily. Arielle: No, especially because we started publishing our Local Changemakers series this week on Wednesday. You can look forward to one Local Changemaker feature every Wednesday in the run-up to Thanksgiving. This week was a little bit different. We have two features because we have the Student Maker story, which kind of inspired us to highlight younger changemakers this year, and then the first nominated Local Changemaker. Karissa: Mm-hmm. I can’t wait to dive into them. But before we do- Mm … that, we wanna remind you that all these solutions are available in our newsletter format, whether you want that every day or just a weekly digest. It’s free to sign up, and the link to do that is in the show notes. Arielle: If you’re more of a social media feed type of news consumer, then you can follow us on all social platforms, @optimistdaily on everything except for X. There we are, @OdeToOptimism. You can also reach me and Karissa directly by emailing us at podcast@optimistdaily.com. We really love getting comments, questions, feedback, or anecdotes that you wanna share with us. So yeah, feel free to shoot us an email whenever. Karissa: We also encourage you to share with friends, loved ones, all this positive news from The Optimist Daily, and remind them that, you know, good things are happening out there in the world. As usual, a big thank you to our Emissaries who financially support the mission of The Optimist Daily. If you would like to become an Emissary, the link to do that is also in the show notes. With all of that said and done, shall we jump into the spooky solutions of the week? Let’s get into it. Age-by-age Halloween tips from a board-certified pediatrician Karissa: The first solution is “Age-by-age Halloween tips from a board-certified pediatrician”. This piece is informed by an actual pediatrician about how to make Halloween work for every kid in your family, and the framing is really specific to each age group in a way that’s genuinely useful. For toddlers, one tip that I thought stood out was to bring a wagon, even if your kid insists they don’t need one when you’re trick-or-treating or attending some kind of Halloween event. For school-aged kids, uh, Dr. Kristen Cook, who is the pediatrician that gives all this advice in the article, frames Halloween as giving earned independence when you’re trick-or-treating, so you can, you know, hang back a couple houses, let the kids lead, but keep them in sight. And then when it comes to teenagers, they might be going to Halloween parties, and at these parties they can come across some peer pressuring situations. It’s good to talk to them about an exit plan for situations they might not be comfortable with and discuss how to deal with these potentially uncomfortable situations, but ultimately trusting them to handle it the right way. So lots of good tips here. This just brings so much Halloween nostalgia back for me. Arielle: Yeah, I, um… my parents didn’t let me participate in Halloween growing up. I know. Heartbreak. I think it just was, uh, you know, we are an immigrant family coming from a very Christian country- Yes, yeah … and they kind of saw it as, like, kind of like devil worship. But, you know, we got over that stage. I was already, um… I kinda aged out of Halloween, uh, in the traditional sense where you go trick-or-treating and all of that. But my youngest sister was able to participate, and she had, like, really fun costumes. As a little kid, she wanted to be a tissue box one year. Um- That’s a good one … which was really weird. It was, like, a High School Musical tissue box, because we had like, High School Musical, um, wrapping paper. And so that’s how she decided to dress up. Karissa: I love it. Arielle: Yeah, so I have vicarious Halloween memories through my youngest sister. Karissa: Well, I mean, as an adult now, maybe you can do some, some of this stuff. NYC food pantries are stocking pet food for struggling households Karissa: The next solution is very heartwarming, and it’s that “New York City food pantries are now stocking pet food for struggling households”. New York State just put $500,000 towards making sure pet owners don’t have to choose between feeding themselves and feeding their animals. There are now 22 food pantries across all five boroughs stocking free pet food, and the reason this program exists is kind of heartbreaking and kind of sweet at the same time. The story mentions a woman named Cassandra in Brooklyn who sometimes eats less so her Shih Tzu doesn’t go hungry, and she’s far from alone. The demand for pet food grew after SNAP benefit cuts, which tells you a lot about just how far those cuts reach into people’s lives. Animal welfare groups have known for years that financial hardship and pet surrender are directly linked, but this program is essentially trying to catch families before they hit that wall. 5 research-backed ways to banish aches and feel better at your desk Karissa: The next solution is a health lifestyle related one, and it’s “Five research backed ways to banish aches and feel better at your desk”. Columbia University researchers ran a study trying to find the minimum effective dose of movement to counteract sitting all day. The answer was actually surprisingly specific. It’s simply five minutes of walking every 30 minutes that makes a difference. NPR actually then tested that with 20,000 of their listeners and found the exact same thing. So this article breaks down that finding plus four other fixes. Arielle, have you ever heard of this tip to walk five minutes every 30 minutes? Arielle: No, but to increase focus, I use the Pomodoro Technique, which is when you set the timer for about 20- 25 minutes and then give yourself a five-minute break. Because I work from home- Yeah … I am always kind of hunched over my laptop. So that is a trick that I use, and I do generally get up and, like, walk around the house. Um- Yeah … so I guess my body intuitively knew that this was a good thing to do, but it’s nice to have the science back it up. Karissa: The whole concept of this kind of, like, movement snack, um, short burst of activity is catching fire and a good suggestion. I guess I’ll mention one more thing about this solution, but you can check out the rest on optimistdaily.com. The whole posture section of this article talks about how the idea of sitting up straight and holding it advice is actually not correct. The actual physical therapist guidance is that your best posture is your next posture, meaning any fixed position causes strain eventually. New Jersey Transit is turning commuter stations into art galleries Karissa: Well, the next solution is “New Jersey Transit is turning commuter stations into art galleries”. NJ Transit has been installing art exhibitions at train and bus stations since 2019, and the program just expanded to its eighth location. The new show is about railroads and 250 years of American history, which is a pretty fun yet informative thing to encounter while you’re just trying to catch your train, the history about railroads. But the whole premise of this is that transit spaces are great for public art because nobody goes there expecting to see any. The encounter is accidental, which makes it different from an intentional gallery visit. I really like this, um, rise of art in public spaces, and it kind of reminds me of a solution we shared a couple months ago about how over in Warsaw they’re putting libraries in commuter stations. So if you have a little time, a layover in transportation, you can go check out the library. So I think this is a really cool kind of global trend. Arielle: And it’s really nice that the program actually pays the artists stipends because public art rarely comes with a real budget, and a lot of the time public art is like a, a mural that maybe someone painted for free or graffiti, which honestly, I’m a huge fan of graffiti. Some of the tags are really impressive, and some of them- Yeah … are just kind of silly, but they’re entertaining in their own way. Um, but that obviously doesn’t come with payment. If anything, it might come with a fine. Karissa: Right. Exactly. In this broader conversation about what public spaces are for, whether that’s a transit station, a library, park, you know, it can be a lot more than just something that people move through. Student Makers: bringing free STEM to students on three continents Karissa: Moving on to the Changemaker series, we talked more about Student Makers in this deeper dive. They are a group bringing free STEM to students on three continents. And like Arielle mentioned, this is the story that made us decide to make the entire series this year about people under 30, because young people are really just doing so many impressive things to change the world. At Student Makers, former students become the instructors. It’s often high schoolers teaching middle schoolers, and the founder’s whole argument is that it’s more relatable to have, um, you know, people who are closer in age to you to help teach things than an adult expert teaching the same material. Like we mentioned, we’ll have some of the main players behind Student Makers on the podcast in the beginning of 2027, which is crazy to even say that 2027 is around the corner. But we look forward to welcoming them on and hearing directly from them. Meet Vivian Ho: the 17-year-old who built a supply network around dignity, not charity Arielle: I will take over from here, Karissa, and my first solution is actually the first nominated changemaker for this series. The title- Ooh … of the article is “Meet Vivian Ho, the 17-year-old who built a supply network around dignity, not charity”. Most programs that distribute supplies to low-income families ask that family to identify themselves before they get anything. So basically, you have to fill out a form, you check a box, you explain your situation to someone with authority over the outcome. Vivian Ho built her nonprofit, All the Same organization, around removing that whole process. Families request what they need anonymously, and nobody has to declare themselves as someone in need to get the help they need. And she started this at just 16, which is quite impressive. Karissa: Mm-hmm. Arielle: The anonymous sign-up system is what makes this really special. Vivian’s read on situations like this was that the stigma of asking for help was keeping families from asking at all. So she just said, “Let’s get rid of that.” There’s also something within this nonprofit. There’s another, uh, initiative called the Cultural Surprises program, and it’s something I hadn’t seen before. So volunteers research the cultural background of the family they’re packing for, and handmade crafts reflecting that culture go out alongside the supply package, and it turns a resource delivery into something more like recognition, something that makes that family feel really seen. I’m not gonna get into all of the details, but I do encourage people who are interested in learning more about Vivian Ho and perhaps how to support her work to check out the article because it is really, really remarkable that she was able to do this as a teenager. Karissa: Congratulations to Vivian for being nominated by two of The Optimist Daily community members who are involved with the project as well, a nomination from her co-founder and a volunteer that she inspired to start his own project nominated Vivian. So go check that out if you wanna learn more. Kenya unlocks $160 million to protect the Maasai Mara and Tsavo ecosystems Arielle: The next solution is titled “Kenya unlocks $160 million to protect the Maasai Mara and Tsavo ecosystems”. Kenya just signed a $160 million deal to protect nearly 67,000 square miles of some of the most important wildlife habitat in Africa, including the Maasai Mara and Tsavo. But the interesting part isn’t just the money, it’s the structure of how that money gets released, because this isn’t a grant that arrives and then disappears. So the funding mechanism is called Project Finance for Permanence. Money flows in tied to specific government policy benchmarks, and not all the money gets, uh, given upfront, let’s say. If Kenya doesn’t hit the milestones, then those funds never get released. Tsavo holds 40% of Kenya’s elephants and 20% of its critically endangered black rhinos, and that’s just to give you an idea of what’s at stake for wildlife and geographically. Kenya committed to the global 30 by 30 target and was sitting at about 20% to 23% coverage, so this deal would largely close that gap by 2030. Will vinegar actually keep bugs out this fall? Pest experts explain what works Arielle: The next solution is titled, “Will vinegar actually keep bugs out this fall? Pest experts explain what works.” So every fall, people reach for the vinegar bottle as a first line of pest defense. They spray the windows, they spray the door frames, and then it feels like they’ve done something. But two pest control experts basically say, “You’ve done nothing.” The reason why is in this article, and there’s also one fall tip in here that’s actually kind of strange and useful. So vinegar unfortunately only kills soft-bodied insects on direct wet contact, and then once it dries, then the vinegar doesn’t really do anything against cockroaches, beetles, spiders, or ants. And researchers found negligible effects on most common household insects. What really works is, like, caulking windows and weather-stripping doors and adding door sweeps. That will actually stop bugs from getting in. Spraying is just treating the symptom and not really addressing the entry point of where all of these pests try to come in and get cozy ’cause the weather outside is getting worse. Um- Yeah … and then the, the weird tip, well, I found it weird or unexpected, is the acorn tip. If you are bringing acorns or pine cones inside this fall, then you should put them in 150-degree Fahrenheit oven for about 30 minutes first, and that will kill whatever’s living inside them, and then you can, like, decorate your home for the holidays in peace knowing that there’s no hidden critter in your pine cone just waiting to make your house their home. Karissa: Exactly. Arielle: The DIY home pest control has surged since the pandemic. People want low-chemical solutions, and that’s why I think vinegar gets so much reach. But yeah, unfortunately it’s just not as effective as everyone thought it was. Karissa: Well, it’s good to know so we don’t waste our vinegar and our time. Arielle: Mm-hmm. Yeah. Karissa: I- I have to say, though, maybe this is bad, but I do like to use just the harsh chemicals and get them out of the way- … if they do come in the house. So I, I don’t hesitate to use the big stuff. Arielle: Yeah. It’s… You know, we appreciate your honesty here. I’m sure there are a lot of listeners who struggle with pests and are like, “Yeah, I’m just gonna obliterate.” The 7 best vegetables to plant if you want to offset rising grocery costs Arielle: The next solution is titled, “The seven best vegetables to plant if you want to offset rising grocery costs”. Grocery prices are unfortunately still high, and two university horticulture experts say there are specific vegetables that genuinely pay for themselves when you grow them at home. Most of the list made sense to me, but there’s one of them that takes three years before it really starts producing, and both experts say plant it anyway. And yeah, there are pretty good reasons, which I will get into. So first, herbs are the economic winner here. They’re among the most expensive produce per ounce at the grocery store. You usually buy more than you use, and growing them means you harvest exactly what you need when you need it. The strange one was the asparagus. It takes two to three years of establishment before you get a real harvest, so you really have to be committed to the asparagus, and also you have to like asparagus. I like asparagus, but I know a lot of people aren’t the biggest fans. But a well-maintained bed produces for up to 20 years. One expert calls it something you’ll have basically for life. Both experts are clear that the garden only saves money if you plant what your household actually eats. So start with vegetables you already go through the most, and that will help you save money in the end. How EV fleets are shielding Europe from oil price volatility Arielle: The last solution that we are gonna share with everyone this week is titled “How EV fleets are shielding Europe from oil price volatility”. So there is that conflict in Iran that has been driving oil prices up 33% this year. But six European countries collectively avoided nearly $2.2 billion in oil import costs just because they have enough EVs on the road. That’s not a projection or a goal, that’s an actual number from a six-month window. Denmark alone displaced 13% of its entire 2025 oil consumption. So there’s a real dollar security argument for EV adoption here that goes beyond anything to do with the environment, although the environment is very important. Karissa: Yes. Arielle: Hopefully this, uh, this will encourage other economies to really invest in their EV development, but also hopefully this conflict ends soon. Karissa: Yeah. So- For multiple reasons, of course. But it just goes to show how moving towards renewable energy, sustainable energy across the board is just the best path towards energy security. Arielle: Definitely. Well, those were all of the solutions we had this week, but before we go, we have a positive quote. Karissa: This week we have, “Part of being optimistic is keeping one’s head pointed toward the sun, one’s feet moving forward.” And that’s from Nelson Mandela. Arielle: Beautiful. Well, everyone, I hope you enjoy your Halloween weekend if you’re celebrating, and if not, then I hope you enjoy the, uh, candy sales that are inevitably- going to happen after Halloween is over. We will both be back next week with more solutions. Karissa: Until then, have a great weekend. items.titleOriginal: What’s the fairest way to tax a hamburger?
items.description: Τα τρόφιμα ευθύνονται για το ένα τρίτο των εκπομπών του θερμοκηπίου της ανθρωπότητας. Και σίγουρα, τα τρόφιμα που εκπέμπουν περισσότερο άνθρακα είναι επίσης αυτά που τείνουν να είναι τα χειρότερα για την υγεία μας, όπως τα κρέατα και τα γαλακτοκομικά. Τι θα γινόταν, λοιπόν, αν προσπαθούσαμε να φορολογήσουμε αυτόν τον άνθρακα, να ωθήσουμε τους ανθρώπους σε δίαιτες υψηλότερων φυτών που είναι πιο υγιεινές για τους ανθρώπους και τον πλανήτη; Μια νέα μελέτη στο Nature Food…
items.descriptionOriginal: Food accounts for a third of humanity’s greenhouse emissions. And sure enough, the most carbon-gushing foods are also the ones that tend to be the worst for our health, such as meats and dairy. So what if we tried taxing that carbon, to nudge people toward higher-plant diets that are healthier for people and planet alike? A new study in Nature Food explores how these food emissions taxes could be applied to countries around the world with different levels of wealth and greenhouse emissions. It shows how they could be tweaked to manage the delicate interplay between food prices, poverty, hunger, and health—while still cutting billions of tons of annual emissions. Economists have estimated that growing populations and increasing meat consumption worldwide could cause the environmental footprint of our food—including greenhouse emissions— to balloon by 50 to 90 percent by 2050 . This has spurred recommendations that humanity shift its diet , toward fewer animals and more plants. Emissions taxes paid by consumers buying foods are one way to encourage a shift away from meats, dairy, eggs , and sugars . But questions remain about how those taxes can be applied fairly to countries around the world—given that wealthier nations have more ability to pay them, and that many of these same nations also contributed disproportionately to rising greenhouse gases in the first place. In the new study, researchers used economic, trade, and public health models to predict how well different types of taxes would curb greenhouse emissions—and also, how they would impact food prices climate policy of all? They compared two tax scenarios. In one, emissions are priced the same worldwide, at a constant cost of USD$ 185 per metric ton of CO 2 equivalent (tCO 2 eq). In this system, wealthy countries would still pay more taxes, because their food systems emit more tons of CO 2 . In the other system, the cost-per-ton of emissions is scaled up or down, based on each country’s wealth—thereby further increasing the taxes paid by consumers in wealthy countries (to as much as $969 per tCO 2 eq), while reducing those paid by lower-wealth countries (to as little as $21 per tCO 2 eq). The researchers compared these two scenarios both with and without a second provision, in which governments would also subsidize fruits and vegetables to further lower the prices that consumers pay for these low-carbon foods. Their results suggest that taxes based on a fixed-price-per-ton would reduce food-related emissions most sharply—by up to 18.7 percent, or about 2.6 billion tCO 2 eq worldwide each year. But such taxes would likely worsen overall health in some countries such as India, Bangladesh, and Vietnam—even after accounting for reductions in heart disease and diabetes—because they might make food less affordable to some people, compromising nutrition. The authors found that adjusting the price-per-ton of emissions based on national wealth would lessen this problem. And subsidizing the cost of fruits and vegetables would further decrease it. Together these two tweaks slightly reduced the emissions that were prevented—but they were still predicted to cut worldwide food emissions by 17 percent, or about 2.3 billion tCO 2 eq per year. The authors recommended that these efforts to reduce the negative impacts on the poor could be further explored, with detailed studies of poverty in individual countries, and potentially by excluding some critical sustenance foods such as fish or rice from the taxes in some countries. Bouyssou, et al. “ Food emissions taxes can deliver health and environmental benefits with limited leakage .” Nature Food , 2026. Image: ©Anthropocene Magazine

items.title: Το κελάηδισμα των πουλιών έχει κοινά χαρακτηριστικά με την ανθρώπινη ομιλία και μουσική – Τι έδειξε επιστημονική έρευνα
items.titleOriginal: Το κελάηδισμα των πουλιών έχει κοινά χαρακτηριστικά με την ανθρώπινη ομιλία και μουσική – Τι έδειξε επιστημονική έρευνα

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Generates Clean Energy, Saves Land, Improves Fishing—What’s Not to Like? Reading Time: 2 minutes In September 2026, solar developer D3 Energy installed a large solar array, not on land or on a rooftop, but on the surface of a reservoir that serves the water needs of the village of Monroeville, Ohio. This floating power plant covers 12 acres of the reservoir’s 16 acres. If a solar facility of this size, which contains 9,220 solar panels, were built on dry land, it would require 30 acres. So doing it the Monroeville way helps to keep open land available for farming, housing, business or industry, conservation land, or any other use. This 6-megawatt installation is projected to generate about 7,500 megawatt-hours of clean electricity to this village of 1,300 residents. Monroeville has already operated a 4-megawatt ground-mounted solar array, built in 2017. This 10-megawatt total gives the town roughly 13 times as much solar-generated power per capita as the rest of Ohio. Their floating solar array is among the five largest in the U.S. In addition to the clean power produced and the avoidance of using land that might be put toward other needed uses, Floato-voltaics projects such as this one have several other benefits. First, the physical barrier created by the floating platforms significantly reduces water evaporation by blocking direct solar radiation and intercepting wind blowing across the water’s surface. Solar “on the water” thereby reduces evaporation by 30% to 80%, depending on temperatures and humidity in the immediate area. The result, depending upon the size of the floating power plant, is an annual savings of millions of gallons of valuable drinking and irrigation water. Beyond clean power, floating solar arrays like Monroeville’s reduce reservoir water evaporation by 30% to 80% by blocking direct solar radiation and wind, saving millions of gallons of drinking and irrigation water annually. Photo courtesy of D3 Energy . Second, by depriving the water of sunlight, there is a sizable reduction of toxic algal blooms. Photosynthetic organisms like blue-green algae require sunlight to thrive. By heavily shading parts of the reservoir, the concentrations of floating solar panels limit the light penetration needed for massive algal blooms. This naturally improves water quality, reducing expenses from chemical treatments needed to purify the water. Third, more fish. During the warmer months, the floating platforms insulate the reservoir’s water against seasonal temperature spikes, helping support cold-water fish species. Local reservoirs are often favorite local fishing spots. And fourth, cleaning issues. Land-based solar arrays, whether in farming or more urbanized areas, often deal with dust, dirt, and other airborne debris. For best panel performance, cleaning of their surfaces in these situations is advisable. Open bodies of water are inherently less affected by blowing dirt and dust, keeping the panels cleaner longer and reducing maintenance costs. All things considered, with all the bodies of fresh water dotting the planet, maybe we should all look more closely for floato-voltaic opportunities just beyond our own backyard. The post Generates Clean Energy, Saves Land, Improves Fishing—What’s Not to Like? appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: I n the early-ish days of Wikipedia, my college friends and I had an ongoing contest to see who could introduce a lie into an entry that would stick the longest. If your goal is to smuggle mistruth into the internet’s encyclopedia, you quickly learn to leave the well-known stuff with hard-and-fast facts alone. Try to change the Battle of Hastings to 1068, or claim Thomas Jefferson wrote Flowers for Algernon , and the Wiki editors swoop in to excise your lies within minutes. It was oddly inspiring to see that the online compulsion to be right, and for things to be right, could become a kind of immune system for upholding the truth. Observing the editors’ behaviors, I conjured up a new strategy. I found a less-trafficked page — the entry for club sandwich — and located a sentence that was already conjecture, and which notably had a citation affixed to its end. The line read: It is thought that the club sandwich was invented in an exclusive Saratoga Springs, New York gambling club in the late 19th Century. I changed this by adding my buddy Danny as the sandwich’s inventor: It is thought that the club sandwich was invented in an exclusive Saratoga Springs, New York gambling club in the late 19th Century by a maverick line cook named Danny Mears. It’s unlikely that John McPhee had stumbled across our Wikipedia sandwich lie when he wrote that “any error is everlasting” in his 2009 New Yorker piece about the magazine’s fact-checking department. But he was right. “Maverick line cook Danny Mears” hardened into sturdier fiction with each repetition, appearing in poorly researched blog posts and online recipes, each mention making the lie seem more true. Wiki editors pulled it down a few times; we snuck it back in. In the end, Mears’ reign as the sandwich’s inventor persisted on Wikipedia for more than three-and-a-half years. An annoyed editor even added a Wiki “talk” comment exposing our misdeeds, titled Danny Mears Did Not Invent It . A couple years later, a friend texted the group to say she’d seen “maverick line cook Danny Mears” go up on the flatscreens as a bar-trivia answer. McPhee goes on to describe the job of fact-checking as a kind of noble guardian, holding back a teeming horde of mistruths: “With drawn sword, the fact-checker stands near the end of this bridge.” We’d camouflaged our lie past a few of these sentries for what amounted to a joyride, but eventually the guards got us. What I’ve been wondering ever since, and especially lately, is: Who’s still guarding that bridge? O ne may initially concede that our defenses seem to be diminishing in the present moment. You don’t have to look far to find a commentator mourning a “post-fact” world or worrying that we swim in toxic waters online when it comes to bad actors and misinformation. Consider that 20 percent of Americans surveyed by Pew Research said they regularly get their news from TikTok, up from three percent in 2020. Last year, Meta ended its U.S. fact-checking program, while the courts have decided that social media platforms are private providers of forums for speech and so can set their own content rules, or remove the guardians from the bridge entirely, depending on their business incentives. Credit: patpitchaya / Shutterstock There are few forces more powerful in the media than a stubborn person on the phone investigating a doubt. In the public sphere of reportage, Duke Reporters’ Lab, which has tracked fact-checking trends for years, found that last year was the first time fact-checking department closures outpaced launches . And on the level of the individual, three-fourths of the fact-checkers surveyed by the International Fact-Checking Network reported being financially vulnerable or in crisis . If the field has had a famous debunker in the last two decades, it has been t he Washington Post ’s Glenn Kessler, who last year accepted a buyout and was not replaced. Should you want to pre-write a eulogy for the capital-T Truth, the material is all here. But fact-checking is not a static field. Like our immune systems, it’s capable of learning and enduring, as well as mobilizing to handle infections of mistruth, which if not treated tend to further polarize voters in political contests. Consider recent false claims from his opponents that Texas Senate candidate James Talarico had disappeared from the campaign trail for mental health treatment at an inpatient facility in Ohio. A high-profile fact-check quickly shifted the narrative from “Talarico is in trouble” to “his opponents look like liars.” (Talarico had the flu and was resting at home, which the New York Times proved by reviewing security camera footage.) Bad-faith punditry has a lessened effect when met with undeniable facts and data, as do the rumors that chip away at our trust in elections themselves. Consider a recent viral video in which a woman from Cook County, Illinois claimed that her voting machine was telling her that her chosen candidate was the less-popular choice. Nonpartisan fact-checks from places like PolitiFact quickly rushed to explain the less-salacious reality: She hadn’t selected enough candidates. Fact-checks can bring the temperature down and reduce our polarization; her town’s Republican Committeeman even rose to refute the claims on Facebook . So while the institutional layer of the media is wounded and we’re ushering in an age of slop and lies, any obituary for the Truth is likely premature. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] “Ever since I was a little kid, I’ve had a thing about wanting to get stuff right,” says Jy Murphy, a freelance fact-checker for the Hearst stable of publications and others. “At this point it bleeds over as a kind of professional deformity.” Murphy tells a simple story set years ago, in which he was fact-checking a Popular Mechanics piece about the freight industry and encountered a confident sentence claiming that nobody double-stacks rail cars in the Eastern U.S. because the bridges were all built with too little clearance. Fact-checkers encounter these offhand assertions all the time: a just-so statement with the ring of a thing that everybody knows. If you were to Google this type of niche knowledge, you might not find anything, and so the fact-checker operates most often as a reporter of the reporting. But after calling the railroad lines themselves, Murphy learned that in the year since the writer had filed the piece, a considerable number of bridges had been raised to allow freight through. The writer’s claim was “either too pessimistic to begin with or had changed in that year,” says Murphy. There are few forces more powerful in the media than a stubborn person on the phone investigating a doubt. It is precisely that thoroughness that makes peer-to-peer fact-checking matter more now in the age of A.I. Of course most large language models (LLMs) can’t yet make phone calls to freight lines, but if I ask Claude about Murphy’s rail bridges I may well still be told that nobody double-stacks rail cars in the Eastern U.S. That model can create a convincing, seemingly well-sourced sentence in a few seconds, but what it is not doing is actually checking the fact . Kelsey Lannin, a Seattle-based fact-checker, tells me that A.I is “very good at aping a confident intellectual on any given topic. But do any amount of work with it and you’ll quickly realize it’s a facade.” She says that it’s better to look at it like having an intern: “You give it an assignment, it gives you something back, and you [still] have to check it.” A.I. boosters may tell you that we’re just getting started, and assure us that this is the worst A.I. will ever be. Nevertheless, A.I. is still failing to produce accurate citations in more than 60 percent of tests, according to a 2025 Tow Center study . Prominent critics say it has nuked the effectiveness of Google and is “ destroying search, the internet and your brain. ” Models create a texture of verification, but they aren’t doing the analog process that makes verification real. If you see a bird out of your window, you can grab an Audubon guide and verify it. Feed a picture of that bird to an LLM and that model is neither “seeing” the chickadee nor “reading” from a primary source specifically. Models produce the most statistically likely next words, but unless prompted, there isn’t a step where Claude or Gemini confirms the truth of its response against the truth of the world. Credit: Andrey_Popov / Shutterstock Fact-checking’s collective response to changing times will continue to be a necessary governor, helping pace our accelerated information environment and dismantle false narratives that fuel polarization. These individual hallucinations and absent citations might seem like drops in a bucket, but they add up to create a rising tide of mistrust in a society already wary of the truthfulness of mainstream media . “What grieves me,” says Murphy, “is how many people think there aren’t [trusted sources].” Still, it is encouraging to see the fact-checking infrastructure responding by adapting to, and building defenses against, this flood. Sometimes, resistance looks like digging in. Inside the same Reporters’ Lab census that tallied closures, we learn that we’ve still got 437 active fact-checking projects around the world, which is just 27 below the all-time high and more than were operating in 2020. Many American newsrooms (North Dakota News Cooperative, CT Mirror in Connecticut and more) have agreed to work with Gigafact , an organization that publishes independently verified “fact briefs.” Wikipedia adopted a stronger A.I.-generated content policy earlier this year, banning LLM-generated content on the site, bar in certain circumstances. And as something becomes perceived to be scarce, it also becomes valuable: A 2026 Reuters study points toward an “increased demand for verification” from readers in a low-trust environment. The most encouraging turn of resistance may be in redirecting the machine back at the onslaught itself. Full Fact , the U.K.’s independent fact-checking charity, is now using A.I. systems to “detect and classify claims across millions of sentences,” per Reuters . A newer version attempts to “prebunk” instead of debunk, creating a model that prioritizes the most potentially damaging narratives for review. A Joint Research Centre study published in Nature investigated and concluded that debunking and prebunking interventions were successful and effective in reducing misinformation’s threats. Like any effort in inoculation, this effort will also need to be collective. At the end of last year, Scott Klein, then-publisher advocate at Newspack, predicted a “return to prioritizing open source collaboration, not as a luxury but as an existential imperative,” highlighting the need for a “show your work” ethos that will help journalism rebuild trust. Full Fact’s tools are being used now by more than 40 organizations across 30 countries, and importantly, the effort is mostly triage. Full Fact offers that the organization will “always keep human experts in the loop, partly to minimise the risks around bias and hallucinations that come with fully-automated systems but mostly because even the most advanced A.I. does not come close to human reasoning.” Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime Sierra Juarez, a fact-checker at NPR’s Planet Money and The Indicator , has another, simpler tip for resistance in the world of misinformation. “If you see something on your social media feed that your gut is telling you seems fishy,” she says, “try to find corroborating evidence in three different sources across different types of publications. Read broadly and try to identify common threads.” Bringing the fact-checker’s stubborn doubt to our daily engagement is available to anyone willing to take a minute before they share a post. Years after my Wikipedia crime spree, I’m heartened that there are fact-checkers out there guarding the bridge and encouraged by the durability of this work. Reports of the Truth’s demise have perhaps been greatly exaggerated. It can be slow and unglamorous, but fact-checking’s collective response to changing times will continue to be a necessary governor, helping pace our accelerated information environment and dismantle false narratives that fuel polarization. “There are,” says Murphy, “good soldiers … a cadre of us out there trying to fight the good fight.” The post Truth, Elections and the Questionable History of the Club Sandwich appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Funding for Indigenous-Led Forest Conservation Gets a New Global Platform Reading Time: 3 minutes Funding for Indigenous-led forest conservation just became easier, as a new UNDP-hosted platform connects private companies and philanthropies directly with the communities protecting many of the world’s most critical forests. Funding for Indigenous-led forest conservation has long faced a structural gap. Indigenous Peoples steward roughly one third of the world’s tropical forests, yet they receive comparatively little political recognition or financial support for that role. Recent climate summits have repeatedly called for Indigenous access to forest tenure rights and climate finance, but turning those pledges into action has proven difficult. A new initiative, Forest Guardians Invest , aims to close that gap directly. Hosted by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), the platform connects private companies, impact investors, and philanthropies with vetted Indigenous-led conservation and bioeconomy projects. Rather than routing funds through layers of intermediaries, the platform creates a more direct financial pathway. Tropical forests play an outsized role in global climate goals. These ecosystems support simultaneous action on climate change, biodiversity loss, and sustainable land management in ways few other landscapes can match. Protecting them effectively requires working with the people who already know these forests best. Many private companies and philanthropies are genuinely willing to fund forest protection through direct partnerships with Indigenous communities. What they typically lack is a reliable, efficient mechanism to do so at scale. Forest Guardians Invest positions itself as that missing mechanism, built specifically around respect for Indigenous rights and international standards. Three core functions define how the funding for Indigenous-led forest conservation platform operates. First, it facilitates financial partnerships between Indigenous Peoples and private companies, ensuring every agreement complies with human rights protections and recognized ESG standards. Second, it monitors private investments in Indigenous-led projects to confirm they deliver the environmental and economic outcomes both parties agreed upon. The platform’s third function focuses on long-term scale. Forest Guardians Invest builds a pipeline of bankable, Indigenous-led bioeconomy projects across forest territories, each with demonstrated climate, biodiversity, and economic results. That pipeline gives investors a clearer picture of opportunities beyond a single pilot project. Partnership models built around free, prior, and informed consent anchor the platform’s approach to Indigenous rights. This framework ensures Indigenous communities retain genuine decision-making power over how their territories and resources get used. Companies gain a trusted gateway to opportunities already vetted for impact and ethical compliance. One early example illustrates how this model works in practice. UNDP partnered with coffee company Lavazza to certify and market the first-ever deforestation-free coffee sourced from Ecuador. That pilot project is now being scaled to additional countries, offering a template for how similar partnerships might expand elsewhere. Harvesting coffee, part of a certified deforestation-free supply chain that shows what funding for Indigenous-led forest conservation can look like in practice. Photo by Carlos Felipe Ramírez Mesa on Unsplash. Founding partner Sacred Forests contributed both funding and a working model during the platform’s design phase. Their approach treats forest conservation itself as a service worth compensating directly, rather than folding it into broader carbon-offset accounting that often overlooks community-level impact. Seed funding from partners like Sacred Forests helped move Forest Guardians Invest from concept to functioning platform. The kind of on-the-ground work this funding for Indigenous-led forest conservation aims to support is already visible across the Amazon. In Brazil’s Maranhão state, a group of Guajajara women known as the Forest Warriors patrol more than 172,000 hectares of the Caru Indigenous Land. They monitor illegal logging, fight wildfires, and combine traditional ecological knowledge with modern tools like drones and GPS mapping. Efforts like theirs demonstrate both the value and the vulnerability of Indigenous-led conservation. Communities already carry out sophisticated, effective forest protection work, often with minimal external funding or formal recognition. Connecting that work to reliable financial support could meaningfully expand its reach and sustainability. Companies and philanthropies interested in engaging with the platform can apply to explore partnership opportunities directly through UNDP’s Climate and Forests initiative. Each partnership gets built around measurable outcomes, giving funders concrete evidence of the climate and biodiversity impact their investment produces. Funding for Indigenous-led forest conservation through platforms like this represents a shift in how global climate finance operates. Rather than treating Indigenous communities as beneficiaries of external programs, this model positions them as direct partners and innovators. That distinction may prove essential for protecting the forests the planet depends on most. The post Funding for Indigenous-Led Forest Conservation Gets a New Global Platform appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News New Map Reveals Natural Forest Regeneration in Tropical Regions Could Absorb 23 Years of Global Emissions Reading Time: 3 minutes A groundbreaking map identifies 215 million hectares suited for natural forest regeneration in tropical regions, capable of sequestering 23.4 gigatons of carbon. For decades, tree planting dominated forest restoration efforts worldwide, despite mounting evidence that a quieter, less expensive alternative often works better. Natural forest regeneration in tropical regions, allowing degraded land to recover on its own with minimal human intervention, frequently produces more biodiverse, resilient forests than plantation-style restoration under similar conditions. Until now, researchers lacked detailed, high-resolution data showing precisely where this natural recovery process holds the greatest promise. A Nature Ecology and Evolution study closed that gap, producing the first model mapping natural forest regeneration potential in tropical regions across every tropical forested country and biome on Earth. Built on remote sensing analysis identifying actual patches of natural forest regrowth between 2000 and 2016, rather than relying on coarse estimates or expert guesswork as previous studies had, the map offers unprecedented precision for targeting restoration investment. The results are striking. Researchers estimate 215 million hectares, an area larger than the entire country of Mexico, hold genuine potential for natural forest regeneration in tropical regions. Left to recover naturally over 30 years, this land could sequester an estimated 23.4 gigatons of above-ground carbon, roughly equivalent to more than two decades of current global emissions from fossil fuels and industry combined. Five countries account for more than half of this global potential. Brazil leads with over 20% of total regeneration potential, followed by Indonesia at nearly 14%, then China, Mexico, and Colombia, rounding out the top five nations that collectively represent 52% of the opportunity worldwide. This concentration suggests that even modest policy shifts within a handful of countries could unlock outsized climate and biodiversity benefits. What distinguishes natural forest regeneration in tropical regions from active planting is cost-effectiveness paired with ecological quality. Rather than purchasing seedlings, preparing sites, and maintaining plantations, natural regeneration often requires simply removing barriers preventing forest recovery, invasive species, unmanaged livestock grazing, or encroaching agriculture, then allowing existing seed banks, root systems, and nearby forest patches to do the rest. Research consistently shows this approach yields forests with greater species diversity and more resilient ecosystem function compared to plantation alternatives. Integrating Indigenous knowledge and securing land rights within these territories increasingly stands out as essential to translating mapped potential into genuine forest recovery. Communities that have sustainably managed these landscapes for generations bring practical understanding of local conditions that purely technical restoration planning cannot replicate on its own. Natural forest regeneration in tropical regions succeeds most reliably near existing forest patches and within territories managed by Indigenous Peoples, whose land stewardship researchers say is essential to translating mapped regeneration potential into genuine, lasting forest recovery. Photo by Bill Salazar on Pexels. The map reveals fine-scale spatial variation researchers say is critical for effective planning. Regeneration potential clusters strongly near existing forest patches, since seed dispersal and ecological connectivity heavily influence whether cleared land can recover naturally. This granular detail lets governments and conservation organizations distinguish between land where natural forest regeneration in tropical regions will likely succeed unaided and land that requires more intensive intervention or active planting. Beyond carbon sequestration, restoring tropical forests at this scale carries far-reaching consequences for biodiversity conservation, since tropical forests harbor a disproportionate share of Earth’s terrestrial species diversity. Millions of livelihoods across forested tropical nations also depend directly on healthy forest ecosystems for food, water regulation, and economic activity, so successful regeneration delivers benefits that extend well beyond atmospheric carbon accounting. Researchers emphasize that the map is intended as a decision-support tool rather than a final policy prescription. Natural forest regeneration in tropical regions succeeds only when paired with appropriate governance structures, including payment-for-ecosystem-services schemes and stronger frameworks that compensate communities for environmental stewardship. The overlap between high-potential regeneration zones and Indigenous Peoples’ territories adds further complexity, since these communities often lack formal land recognition despite serving as effective forest stewards in practice. As nations pursue ambitious global restoration commitments under frameworks addressing both climate change and biodiversity loss, this map offers something previously unavailable: precise, evidence-based guidance on where natural forest regeneration in tropical regions could deliver the greatest return on conservation investment. Rather than treating forest restoration as a uniform global strategy, the research points to a more targeted approach, one that recognizes that some degraded tropical land wants only the chance to heal itself, provided the barriers standing in its way are finally removed. items.descriptionOriginal: For 42 years, Peter navigated a world built on words he couldn't read -- memorizing road signs, mapping routes in his mind, quietly relying on his wife -- until a moment of panic in a supermarket aisle, afraid he might accidentally poison his family with the wrong milk, made it impossible to keep going as before. What followed was three years of twice-weekly sessions with a volunteer named Alison, working through reading manuals slowly and without judgment, until the world, as Peter puts it, "completely opened up." His goal had been to read the first Harry Potter book, drawn to Harry as a fellow outsider, and he finished it. The story sits with you not because of how far Peter came, but because of how long he carried something so heavy so quietly -- and how, in the end, it was a wife's steady presence, a stranger's patience, and his own willingness to try one more time that made the difference. "I can't believe how beautiful reading is," he says now, and the wonder in that sentence belongs to anyone who has ever arrived somewhere they once thought was not meant for them.

items.descriptionOriginal: This article was written by Jeff LeBlanc , a learning facilitator for online master of business administration at Boston University, for The Conversation — a nonprofit news organization dedicated to sharing the knowledge of researchers and scientists, under a Creative Commons license . Read the original article here . For all the talk about generational differences at work, some of the biggest differences show up in surprisingly ordinary moments. Take being late for work. A Gen Z employee in her 20s I spoke with works at a small, locally owned café and restaurant run by an older Gen X owner. When she realized she was going to be late one day, she texted him. He was frustrated. To him, being late was serious enough to warrant a phone call, and a text felt too casual and impersonal. She saw the exact same interaction very differently. “He’s super busy, so I felt a call was going to take up too much time,” she told me. “So I texted. I thought it was more considerate.” Both thought they understood what respectful workplace communication looked like. They just had completely different definitions of it. I study workplace culture and communication, and I see this type of misunderstanding as increasingly common in multigenerational workplaces. And this is becoming more pronounced as Gen Z moves further into the workforce. The oldest members of Gen Z are now approaching 30, while the youngest are in college and high school. What’s distinctive about the older members of Gen Z is that many went through college, internships or their first jobs during the COVID-19 pandemic , when much of our communication moved online and masks often covered half our faces. And there’s a new twist now, as artificial intelligence changes how we communicate all over again. The result isn’t necessarily that Gen Z employees communicate better or worse with their bosses and colleagues than previous generations did. I argue that they have simply learned to do so in a very different environment. When a Text Means Something More The café example is an easy one to dismiss as younger workers preferring texting and feeling that phone calls are for important occasions only. But that misses what I think is the more interesting point: The employee wasn’t trying to avoid her boss. She thought she was respecting his time. For her boss, by contrast, the phone call itself carried meaning. It communicated that she understood the seriousness of being late. Neither one had explained that expectation to the other. Managers shouldn’t assume employees attach the same meaning they do to a particular form of communication. If being late requires a phone call, they need to say so. A two-minute conversation about expectations can prevent both people from walking away from an interaction believing the other was disrespectful. Another common stumble concerns openness, which might feel like oversharing. One Gen Z worker I spoke with had recently started a job at a large New England company in a blue-collar industry. He was struggling with severe anxiety and decided to tell his baby boomer manager. The manager was sympathetic, but also uneasy. “It made me feel uncomfortable, if I’m being honest,” the manager told me. “I didn’t want to downplay his anxiety, but I’m not sure I needed to know.” That distinction matters. His reaction wasn’t that anxiety wasn’t real or that his employee should simply get over it. But he questioned how much of it belonged in their professional relationship. Many older workers learned that professionalism is about setting clear boundaries between personal and professional life. Members of Gen Z are coming of age during a period when conversations about mental health and personal well-being are considerably more public. What feels like honesty to one person can feel like oversharing to their boss. This doesn’t mean that managers have to become therapists, and employees don’t have to disclose everything happening in their lives. But both may need to recognize that their comfort level around disclosure isn’t universal. Aleksandra Sapozhnikova on Unsplash, CC BY What younger workers may see as honesty could be seen as oversharing by older colleagues, who tend to keep more boundaries over personal information. Learning to Read a Room When the Room Disappeared Some workplace communication is never spoken at all. Think about how people traditionally learned to read a room. They watched faces around a conference table. They noticed a change in a manager’s tone. Someone caught them after a meeting and quietly explained what had just happened. Now think about someone who was 18 or 19 in 2020. At exactly the age when many young people would have been developing these skills in college, internships and early jobs, the room disappeared. Classes went online. Internships became remote. When people returned in person, masks sometimes made facial communication more difficult. That doesn’t mean members of Gen Z can’t read facial expressions, but we should be careful about assuming everyone had the same opportunities to learn the unwritten signals of professional life. If feedback matters, I believe managers should say it. A disappointed expression on a Zoom call is a poor substitute for a conversation. I Thought That Was Understood Imagine a manager telling a young employee: “I need this by Friday.” The employee sends it back at 4:30 p.m. that Friday afternoon. The manager is annoyed because they intended to review it that morning, make changes and send it along to someone else. The employee is equally confused. The deadline was Friday, and they met it. This deadline mismatch gets at something I have repeatedly encountered in my research with Gen Z workers. In a survey I conducted of 250 Gen Z professionals across industries, clear structural expectations emerged alongside fairness and empathetic engagement as recurring themes. If an employee wants clarity , it shouldn’t automatically be confused with hand-holding. An employee can want autonomy and still want to know exactly what success looks like. “Friday” and “Friday by 10 a.m. because I need three hours to review this” communicate very different expectations. Artificial intelligence may make this issue even more important. We can now produce polished emails, summarize meetings and generate information faster than ever. But more communication does not guarantee more understanding. I believe that may be the larger lesson for every generation working together. We tend to mistake the workplace norms we learned for common sense. They aren’t. They were taught to us by the workplaces, technologies and moments in history in which we began our careers. Gen Z is learning theirs in a very different world. RELATED: In New Book, Therapist Defines 5 Communication Types — Here’s Why It Helps to Know Yours

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM A new analysis by energy think tank Ember finds that six European countries collectively avoided close to $2.2 billion (approximately €2 billion) in oil import costs between March and August 2026. The savings came directly from EV fleets reducing how much oil those countries needed to import. Those numbers land differently now that oil prices have climbed 33 percent since the Iran conflict began in late February 2026. Brent crude traded near $100 a barrel in late October, up from $67 before hostilities started. Iran’s control of the Strait of Hormuz, a 104-mile (167-kilometer) shipping channel carrying about one-fifth of the world’s daily oil and liquefied natural gas supply, has been the main reason why. Europe’s share of a $20 billion shift Globally, the EV boom displaced an estimated 200 million barrels of crude oil, worth around $20 billion, over those six months. China accounts for the largest share: its fleet of roughly 44 million EVs saved $14 billion in oil costs. EU member states accounted for another $3.1 billion. Within Europe, Germany and France led on raw savings, at around $760 million and $560 million respectively. Denmark’s numbers told a different story. Its EV fleet displaced 6.4 million barrels of oil per year as of August 2026, equal to 13 percent of the country’s entire 2025 oil consumption, the highest share in Europe. The UK displaced around $790 million in crude over the six months; the country imported roughly $27 billion (approximately £21.5 billion) worth of crude in the preceding year. The security dividend Global EV sales grew 11 percent year-on-year in the first eight months of 2026, while combustion engine vehicle sales fell six percent. “The countries that invested in EVs before this crisis are now better protected,” said Euan Graham, a senior energy analyst at Ember, “and a growing number are following.” An EV doesn’t run on oil. At national scale, that translates to real insulation from price shocks driven by conflict or supply disruptions. “Every EV on the road reduces exposure to volatile oil markets,” Graham said, “and as fleets grow, so does the protection against future supply shocks.” The countries that invested in EVs before oil prices climbed now have a specific dollar figure for what that looked like. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Not every vegetable belongs in a backyard garden. Some take up space, demand attention, and still cost more to grow than to buy once you factor in seeds, soil, and the time it takes. But some crops genuinely save you money, and if your grocery bill has been creeping up, those are the ones to plant. Robert Westerfield , a horticulture specialist at the University of Georgia , and Damon Abdi , assistant professor at the Louisiana State University AgCente r, both weigh in on what pays off at home. Seven vegetables made the list. Herbs Westerfield describes herbs as “so forgiving,” and the economics back that up. Fresh herbs are among the most expensive produce per ounce at the grocery store, and a purchased bunch often goes partly to waste before you get through it. A plant in your garden means you take what you need, when you need it, and nothing wilts in the back of the drawer. Rosemary is an especially smart first choice. It’s evergreen, drought-tolerant, and flowers in a way that looks good in the garden, not just the kitchen. Abdi recommends it specifically because you can harvest on demand rather than buying packaged herbs that “can languish if left unused.” Peppers Peppers are resilient in a way that a lot of vegetables aren’t. Westerfield calls them cold-hardy and says they “come through disease and insects better than anything.” They need consistent water and well-draining soil, but they produce over a long season, and fresh peppers aren’t cheap. Tomatoes Cherry tomatoes are the easiest entry point. Westerfield recommends starting with one or two plants, which he says will supply you through the season with “less trouble than the larger ones.” Give them a trellis or something to climb and they’ll mostly look after themselves. Green beans Green beans can be seeded directly into the ground, no transplants needed, and they produce heavily once they get going. “If you take care of them, you can harvest into the summer,” Westerfield says. They’re a forgiving crop and a reliable one, which makes them a sensible place to start. Asparagus Asparagus is a different kind of investment. Both Westerfield and Abdi recommend it, but the payoff takes patience. The first year or two are about establishment. By the third and fourth year, the harvest grows. A well-maintained bed can produce for up to 20 years. “Asparagus is pricey up front and takes a little time and effort, but it’s perennial once you get it established,” Westerfield says. “You’ll have it basically for life. They can keep on loving you as long as you love them.” Abdi notes that asparagus does best where winters are cool, and that gardeners in warmer climates should look for cold-hardy varieties bred for those conditions. Cucumbers Cucumbers produce heavily and pickle well, so a good summer harvest can stretch well into winter with a few jars on the shelf. Keep them off the ground by growing vertically, and they’ll stay healthier through the season. Squash Squash is easy to grow, though squash bugs and squash vine borers can derail a season quickly if you let them get ahead of you. Stay on top of those two pests, and you’ll come away with a solid harvest. One honest caveat Westerfield is all in on home growing, but he’s clear-eyed about the work involved. It takes time, effort, and real upfront cost. “You know what you put on it and you know where it comes from,” he says. “Usually, the taste and quality are outstanding. There’s nothing quite like fresh tomatoes and sweet corn out of the garden.” The garden only saves money if you’re harvesting and eating what you planted, so starting with the vegetables your household already goes through most is how you make sure it does. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Renewable Natural Gas Is Turning Everyday Waste Into Cleaner Fuel for Businesses Reading Time: 3 minutes Renewable Natural Gas Is Turning Everyday Waste Into Cleaner Fuel for Businesses The shift towards sustainability has led to numerous innovations in the way that companies operate. One of the most exciting developments is the use of renewable natural gas (RNG). RNG is created by capturing methane from sources such as agricultural runoff, landfills, and wastewater treatment plants. This not only reduces the amount of greenhouse gases released into the atmosphere but also creates a new source of energy for those facilities. Adding RNG to your natural gas procurement for businesses is a straightforward way to hit green targets without risking downtime. It tackles organic waste head-on and acts as an easy, drop-in replacement for fossil fuels. How Everyday Waste Transforms into Power The journey from refuse to resource is a fascinating one that involves the capture and processing of methane gas from decomposing organic matter before it escapes into the atmosphere. Instead of allowing this potent greenhouse gas to contribute to climate change, facilities that use anaerobic digesters are able to break down dairy manure, food scraps, and wastewater sludge. The biogas that is produced from these facilities undergoes a purification process to remove moisture, carbon dioxide, and other elements from the gas. The resulting gas is structurally identical to natural gas, allowing it to be injected into existing gas infrastructure and utilized by commercial fleets and manufacturing plants without any need for modification to their equipment. Evaluating the Financial and Environmental Dual Benefits Shifting to this circular energy model offers companies a unique opportunity to tackle two major corporate objectives simultaneously: minimizing ecological impact and stabilizing operational costs. Because RNG is domestically produced from continuous waste streams, it can help shield commercial consumers from the extreme price volatility often associated with global fossil fuel markets. When executives sit down to analyze their overall natural gas procurement strategies, incorporating a renewable component proves highly advantageous for long-term budget forecasting. Furthermore, utilizing this upgraded biogas significantly lowers a company’s direct carbon footprint, allowing brands to authentically market their sustainability achievements to an increasingly eco-conscious consumer base. Overcoming Adoption Barriers and Infrastructure Myths One of the most common misconceptions about the implementation of alternative fuels is that companies will have to invest millions of dollars into new machinery and infrastructure. However, since the upgraded biomethane is chemically identical to the geological methane that now fuels the majority of the nation’s cities and industries, the fuel can be easily implemented into the existing pipeline system without any need for the implementation of new machinery or infrastructure. Also, since the fuel is chemically identical to the existing fuel, the implementation of this new fuel source will not require the implementation of new infrastructure. Instead, the companies can simply update their purchasing agreements with the companies that produce the fuel to implement the new fuel source into their operations. Strategic Sourcing for Corporate Sustainability Goals A sophisticated strategy is needed to source sustainable energy, especially given the growing demand for environmentally friendly substitutes in a number of heavy industries. To make sure they are obtaining genuine environmental attributes in addition to their physical fuel supply, corporate buyers must negotiate a complicated web of producers, marketers, and local utility regulations. When handling natural gas procurement for businesses, look for suppliers who can trace their biomethane straight from the farm or landfill to your facility. Securing these transparent contracts makes it much easier to prove emission cuts to stakeholders and meet strict climate regulations. Embracing the Circular Economy of Tomorrow Another way in which the use of upgraded biogas can benefit commercial enterprises is in reducing their reliance on traditional fossil fuels. The use of biogas as a fuel source for these companies can help to significantly reduce their carbon footprint without any changes to their daily operations. As the technology to capture and refine methane improves, the availability and affordability of biogas will continue to increase. Companies that incorporate biogas into their energy portfolios will be at an advantage compared to their competitors who do not take such steps towards sustainability. The post Renewable Natural Gas Is Turning Everyday Waste Into Cleaner Fuel for Businesses appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Compostable plastics are touted as a greener alternative to conventional petroleum-based plastics that can linger in the environment for centuries. But there’s a catch. Degradable plastics only break down in the right conditions typically found in a composting facility. The tons of compostable plastic that ends up in oceans can still float around for decades and threaten marine life and ecosystems. Researchers have found a way for plastics to break down much faster in the ocean. They embedded tiny amounts of plastic-degrading enzymes in compostable polyester plastics. The enzyme-containing polyesters completely degraded in a relatively short time period even in microbe-scarce environments. The method works at all depths from coastal waters to the deep open sea, the researchers report in the journal Nature . There are many types of biodegradable plastics in commercial use today. These plastics are designed to decompose completely by microorganisms at certain temperatures and humidities . Those conditions are found in industrial composting facilities and with more care in backyard compost settings. But out in cold ocean water, biodegradable plastics can persist for a long time. The research team from Japan took four types of compostable plastic—PBS, PBSA, PCL, and PBAT—and melted them. The heat of the melt would destroy plastic-degrading enzymes . So the researchers made freeze-dried forms of Candida antarctica lipase B and Humicola insolens cutinase enzymes.
