After sealing the samples in a polyethylene meshes, they placed the meshes at various locations off the coast of Tokyo, ranging in water depths from 2–6 m to 5,503 m. They monitored the samples over periods ranging from one month to 18 months. At 757 m, PBS, PBSA and PCL films containing 3% cutinase nearly completely disappeared within five months. Films of those three plastics containing only 0.1 wt% cutinase lost 27.4%, 100% and 85.5% of their mass, respectively, in 1 month. And enzyme-containing plastics also showed moderate biodegradation on the cold floor of the deepest test site. Meanwhile, microbeads embedded with 0.1 wt% cutinase formed visible pores and cracks within 2 weeks in coastal seawater. “These results demonstrate enzyme embedding as a material-level strategy to enhance the environmental degradability of the compostable polyesters…across diverse marine environments without compromising their mechanical properties,” the researchers write. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Removing Forever Chemicals from Farmlands Gets Easier with New Eco-Friendly, Affordable Method Reading Time: 3 minutes A new Yale-led study finds that removing forever chemicals from farmlands could become far cheaper using hemp, rock dust, and biochar, potentially cleaning contaminated soils within a decade. Removing Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS) from farmlands could soon become far cheaper and far less destructive. A new Yale-led study outlines a three-step process using plants, rock dust, and biochar. Researchers say it could work within a single decade. The chemicals in question are often called “forever chemicals.” They resist breaking down and have built up in soil for decades. Much of that contamination traces back to sewage sludge once used as fertilizer. Removing forever chemicals from farmlands matters because these chemicals do not simply fade away on their own. Once present in soil, they can persist for generations without intervention. That persistence is part of why the chemicals earned their nickname in the first place. The study estimates PFAS have contaminated roughly 1.2 million hectares of U.S. cropland. Some Maine farms have already shut down after soil tests exceeded safety limits. Exposure to these chemicals has been linked to certain cancers, thyroid problems, and fertility issues. Health researchers have also linked long-term PFAS exposure to weakened immune response. These risks make removing forever chemicals from farmland a public health priority, not just an environmental one. Farmers directly exposed to contaminated soil and water face some of the highest risks. Conventional cleanup methods of removing forever chemicals from farmlands usually means excavating and burning contaminated soil entirely. That approach can cost an estimated $1.6 million per hectare. Scaled nationally, the total bill could reach roughly $8 trillion. The Yale team’s model instead starts with basalt rock dust spread across farmland. This dust shifts soil pH in a way that sounds counterproductive at first. It actually makes PFAS more available for uptake by nearby plants. Hemp and certain perennial grasses then draw the loosened PFAS out of the soil. Rock dust sped up removal of one compound, called PFOS, by 20-40%. Researchers call PFOS the higher regulatory priority of the two chemicals studied. Harvested plants next go through a heating process to make biochar. That heat destroys much of the remaining chemical structure left in the plant tissue. Spreading the finished biochar back onto contaminated fields could cut chemical runoff by 95%. A Yale-developed process for removing forever chemicals from farmlands uses basalt rock dust to loosen chemical bonds in contaminated soil, allowing hemp (photo above) and perennial grasses to draw pollutants up through their roots before harvesting and heating the plants into biochar that, spread back onto fields, could cut PFAS runoff by 95%. Photo by Mark Stebnicki on Pexels. Postdoctoral researcher Jake Thompson led the study alongside professor Noah Planavsky at Yale. Planavsky, who comes from a farming family, says farmers urgently need better tools to address this problem. Thompson notes that small and organic farms were often hit hardest by past PFAS-laden fertilizer use. Combined, researchers project these steps could bring soils below safety thresholds within a decade. Estimated costs come in at around $1,460 per hectare each year. That figure is a tiny fraction of traditional excavation and burning costs. The rock dust and biochar processes also carry an added climate benefit. Both methods help pull carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere over time. Scaled nationwide, researchers estimate the approach could remove 10.5 million metric tons of carbon dioxide each year. Unlike excavation, this method would let farmers keep working their land throughout the process. Researchers note that removing forever chemicals from farmlands is a global issue beyond the United States. In parts of Europe and the UK, most sewage sludge still gets applied directly to farmland. Europe alone spreads about 10 million tons of sewage sludge onto cropland each year. The United Kingdom applies sludge to roughly 70% of its farmland. China follows a similar pattern, researchers say, making the contamination problem a shared one worldwide. So far, the findings come from computer modeling built on real farm data rather than full field trials. The research team now hopes to test the approach on partner farms across different soil types. Real-world results of removing forever chemicals from farmlands through this approach will show whether these modeled gains hold up outside the lab. If they do, hemp, rock dust, and biochar could offer struggling farmers a genuine way forward. For land written off as unusable, that alone would count as real progress. The post Removing Forever Chemicals from Farmlands Gets Easier with New Eco-Friendly, Affordable Method appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: I n 1991, Saskia Sassen published The Global City in which she asserted that London had more in common with New York and Tokyo than it did with other parts of the U.K. The geography of culture wasn’t delineated by national borders, she argued — there was no need to travel across an ocean to experience ways of life vastly different from your own. That ethos is embodied by American Exchange Project, an intercultural exchange program for youth that takes place entirely within the United States. The exchanges send students who have just graduated high school on weeklong sojourns to U.S. communities completely different from their own. Participating students then host a cohort of peers in their own town, creating a true interchange of American experiences. For many of these students, the exchange is not only an opportunity to see a different part of the country, but to have deep discussions with their new friends about how their lives are different — and the same. “I hadn’t really experienced something where the point of spending time together was to talk about this big, deep stuff,” says Alden Swanson, a student from Chestertown, Maryland whose exchange took place in Orem, Utah. “And that led to so many interesting conversations about differences, but also brought up a lot of similarities about beliefs and how we thought about the world.” Interactions like these are becoming rarer, as Americans increasingly choose to live in cities and towns where their neighbors hold views similar to their own. According to Bill Bishop, author of The Big Sort: Why the Clustering of Like-Minded America Is Tearing Us Apart , the share of voters living in “landslide counties” — where a presidential candidate won by 20 or more points — rose from about 26 percent in 1976 to more than 60 percent in 2016. People are proactively moving to communities with less political and cultural heterogeneity. More than two out of five Americans consider it important that their neighbors share their politics, according to Bishop. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] That said, American Exchange Project makes it clear that these exchanges aren’t about exposing students to new political views (any more than a foreign exchange program would primarily be about politics). Instead, they’re a rare opportunity to immerse young people in an unfamiliar American context and help them build empathy for those whose communities and cultures diverge from their own. Sunny Beam, a student from Ilwaco, Washington, had never spent time in a place with a population of more than 10,000 people before her exchange sent her to the Bronx in New York City. “It’s not even comparable to the places I lived before. It was so nice,” she says. “You’d think that living in a small town, everyone’s super closely knit together, but that’s not always a good thing.” The culture shock of being transported from small town to booming metropolis was offset by the hospitality she was shown by a city used to embracing people of all stripes. Alden Swanson and some of her American Exchange Project peers. Courtesy of Alden Swanson “Because everyone didn’t know everyone else, you would think that they’d be super-standoffish, but everyone was just incredibly welcoming, even to strangers,” she says. “It felt more community-based than my town because everyone was so welcoming and everyone was so willing to, like, work with the diversity rather than shut people out.” For Andrew Wood from Kilgore, Texas, who was also sent to New York, one of the biggest lessons of the exchange was that connecting across cultures needn’t be complicated. “I’m a person who likes to bring the group together,” says Wood. “And so as soon as we got there, I’m like, ‘Okay, guys, you want to play some UNO? Because they got UNO cards for us.’ And so we decided to play UNO, and we started talking and getting to know each other, and we kind of just really clicked from there.” The post The Student Exchange Program That Never Leaves the U.S. appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .
